_doc: The people of Salt Creek (#1309, Sean 2026-11-27): one sheet a person, keyed by the roster's id (config/valley_folk.json's `id`: the game, the missions and the tests use those ids, so a name is a field here, never a new id). `aliases`: roster ids that are the same man as another entry. Each sheet: `kind` (townsfolk: this file's proposal, Sean's to OK on the People board; cast: a mission's character, only what the bible fixes, not renamed; sean: written by Sean, his facts fixed), `role`, `name` (null: roles only, C14 c), `called` (what the town calls him), `who` (one line), `age`, `born`, `from`, `came` (why he came), `work`, `place` (his place in town), `wants`, `secret` (one fear or secret), `likes` / `dislikes` ([{id, why}], ids of this file), `habit` (something the player can see), `talks` (how he talks: plain notes), `voice` (the casting brief), `body` and `clothes` (#1207: a shared body type, clothes by trade), `lines` (samples in his own voice: `id`, `place` (a tag of `places`, the same tag #1293's overheard talk and the game use), `to` (an id, or absent: anyone in earshot), `when` (only if it needs something to have happened), `words`, `src` (cast only: built / script / bible)), `seen` (cast with no day: where the story puts him), `day_proposed` (in words, only for a man not in valley_folk.json yet), `fixed` ({field: where it's fixed}: the bible's or Sean's; every other filled field is PROPOSED by #1309; a null field is open), `notes` (for the next writer). No line says Harlan's name (#1207), but the built ones. The board (docs/story/board/build_people.py, people_board.html) is built from this file and config/valley_folk.json; `python3 docs/story/board/build_people.py --check` checks ids, places and line ids. MORE (Sean, 2026-11-27, #1309's later comments), each its own folded section on the board: `in_town` (how long, how he came, what he's seen change, what he did before), `circle` ({friends, family}), `home` ({what, state: built | to be built (against config/valley.json), where}), `if_dies` ({grief, lines: [{id, by (a person's id), words}], bearers, after}), `knows` ([{what, from (when he has it), tells (whom), takes (trust, money or a threat)}]: nobody gives away one of VOICES.md's secrets before its beat), `trouble` (his nerve, nosy and duty dials in words), `harlan` ({starts, warms, cools, greets: {warm, wary, cold, afraid}}: TownRegard's four bands), `jobs` (small happenings he could bring the deputy), `looks` ({body, hair, beard, clothes, wear}), `casting` ({voice, accent, pace, say_name}), `owns` ({money, home, pockets, owes}), `week` ({sunday, payday, vices}), `loyalty` ({side, why}: where he stands with the Baron). A sheet without them is not written yet (`more_done` lists who has them). Top level `nobody_knew`: the shared card of funeral lines for a stranger, a gang's rider and a known outlaw.
status: PROPOSED (#1309, 2026-11-27): every townsperson's name and sheet waits on Sean's Person OK on the People board. The cast's sheets hold only what the bible fixes. Claude Bérubé is Sean's (#1207). Read blind once (DIALOGUE.md section 4) on 2026-11-27 and re-worded: buttons, threes and writer's jokes cut, the voices pulled apart. The fourteen further sections (Sean, 2026-11-27) are written for the saloon's regulars and Claude Bérubé (`more_done`); the rest of the town's are the next session's. The town drunk (Sean, 2026-11-27) is added as a new person, `town_drunk`, with a full card; his notes about town and the mocking as a mechanic are #1312's.
assumed: The railroad reached Salt Creek in 1881: Claude Bérubé hauled his press in by freight wagon in 1880 (Sean, #1207), and the trains run in the missions. The teamster's and the livery man's sheets lean on it.
The general store holds the valley's mail (most stores of the time did): the storekeeper's wife's sheet leans on it.
The roster's miner is written so he could be Buried Alive's miner (VOICES.md: no name, C14 c, 'maybe Cornish'), but that is not decided; if he is, his name here is a proposal for that man too.
The loudmouth could be 'the loudest man at the rope' (VOICES.md, Smaller voices); not decided, and nothing here depends on it.

places.saloon.table: The saloon: the card table and the tables
places.saloon.room: The saloon: the piano corner and the floor
places.store: The general store (inside, its walk and its bench)
places.hotel: The hotel (its table, its porch and its walk)
places.out: Out of town (the ranches, the mine, the creek, the roads)

barkeep.called: the barkeep; nobody in a script names him
barkeep.who: Owns the saloon, hears everything, and sells it to whoever pays.
barkeep.came: Sold whiskey out of a tent to the railroad's graders and stayed when the camp turned into a street; the saloon and its new dance hall are his.
barkeep.work: Behind his bar from ten in the morning till three; he never leaves it.
barkeep.wants: To be paid: for the chair, for the glass, for what he heard. Tonight, his four dollars.
barkeep.secret: What he was paid not to see. He takes the foreman's money to look into the till at the right moment, and he hasn't asked himself what for.

likes.why: Never once took a drink on the house: he'd pour it and Earl would leave the dime.
She brings the room to the bar and never drinks his profit.

dislikes.why: Thirty-one dollars on the slate, worked off in gossip.
Prints for a nickel what he sells for a dollar.
Breaks furniture.

barkeep.habit: Prices whatever a man is leaning on. Wipes the bar toward himself, as if raking it in.
talks: Aggrieved and quick; every sentence has a sum in it.
Calls every man by his name: he knows them all.
Swears by Jesus and God, in front of anybody.
barkeep.voice: Forties; a nasal Midwestern voice that rises when he's upset.
barkeep.clothes: White shirt, black vest, sleeve garters, an apron he wipes his hands on.

lines.words: Jesus, Cody, my chair!
Somebody ought to fetch the... hell. Ain't nobody left to fetch.
Never once took a drink on the house. I'd pour it and he'd leave the dime.
That's three, Jory. I'm counting if you ain't.
God damn it, Rufe, set it down like you paid for it. Them glasses is nine cents landed.
Thirty-one dollars, Rufe. I got it wrote down in two places.
Kitty. Table by the window's got money and no company.

lines.when: after the drunk has first called you Brevet
lines.words: Brevet's Army talk. Rank with no pay to it. He means you got the badge and not the wages. He ain't wrong, is he?

fixed.name: roles only (C14 c): he is in No Law's script, so no name until Sean gives one
fixed.who: DESIGN.md: 'hears everything, sells it to whoever pays'
fixed.secret: VOICES.md: 'What he was paid not to see' (whether he knows the stranger for the foreman is the script's, K11)

barkeep.notes: Everything else (Peoria, the tent, the sums) is proposed. He calls the townsfolk by the names in this file.
barkeep.in_town: Three years, since the grade. He came with the railroad's graders in 'seventy-nine, alone, selling whiskey from a tent; put up the saloon's front in 'eighty and the dance hall since. He has seen the camp become a street, the mine's payday become his best night, and the Baron's riders become his best customers. Before: bottle-washer and then barman at Peoria; a sutler's clerk in the war.

circle.friends: None: he is behind his bar from ten till three. Kitty and Stiles are his people. He does his books at the bar's end of a morning. He shuts for a burying and comes up late with his apron on.
circle.family: A sister in Peoria. He sent her a photograph of the saloon.

home.what: Over the saloon.

if_dies.grief: The saloon is shut, and the town finds it has nowhere to be.

lines.words: He kept a saloon, and he and I did not agree about it. Every burying I've read in this town, he shut his doors and stood at the back with his apron still on, there, by the gate.
Himself took his share off the top, and it was the share he said it would be. I've worked for worse.
Docked me the slow nights, regular. The winter I had the pleurisy he paid me the whole of it and said it was a mistake in the book.

if_dies.bearers: Trembath, Mapes, Yount, Stroud, Hollis, Burdett.
if_dies.after: The saloon stays shut until somebody buys it at the sale, and the Railroad Saloon has the town's trade. (Payday Night needs him alive: this is for after it.)

knows.what: Who drinks with whom; Cody by name; the day the payroll comes; and what he was paid not to see.
knows.tells: whoever pays
knows.takes: Money. Trust buys nothing here, and a threat gets the cheap half. (The bible's; whether he knows the stranger for the Baron's foreman is the script's: K11.)

knows.what: The sawn floor: nothing. It is his own floor.

barkeep.trouble: Nerve 0.7, nosy 0.4, duty 0.6. He stays behind the bar. His first words are for the furniture, his second send somebody for the doctor. He doesn't run and doesn't draw.

harlan.starts: Wary: a customer who drinks little.
harlan.warms: Breakage paid for; Cody taken without the room being wrecked.
harlan.cools: Broken furniture; the riders' trade driven off.

greets.warm: Deputy. This one's mine to stand.
greets.wary: Deputy. What'll it be?
greets.afraid: Not in here. Please, Deputy. Outside.

jobs: A drummer left owing for three nights' whiskey and a broken lamp.
Somebody is watering his barrels, and it isn't him.
He wants Rufe's slate collected, or Rufe frightened.

looks.hair: Thin, oiled, parted in the middle.
looks.clothes: White shirt, black vest, sleeve garters, an apron he wipes his hands on.
looks.wear: A wet apron, bitten nails, slate-pencil dust on his fingers.

casting.voice: Forties; a nasal Midwestern voice that rises when he's upset.
casting.pace: Quick; it rises when he's upset.

owns.money: The till, and a strongbox under the floor behind the bar. On paper he is the richest man on the street after Hollis.
owns.home: A bed, a ledger, a framed licence.
owns.pockets: Keys, a slate pencil, a bung starter in reach.
owns.owes: A note on the dance hall, at the bank.

week.sunday: Open from noon.
week.payday: Every hand he has, and the dance hall.
week.vices: None. He doesn't drink his own stock.

loyalty.side: paid by him, in small sums
loyalty.why: He takes the foreman's money for small blindnesses and sells to anybody. Nobody's man, and everybody's.

miner.name: Jory Trembath
miner.called: Jory; 'Cousin Jack' to men who don't know him
miner.who: A Cornish hard-rock man, thirty-nine years underground, who drinks his shift down at the bar and knew what Earl was.
miner.from: St Just, Cornwall; tin at fourteen
miner.came: Tin failed at home. Copper on the Keweenaw, then gold at Central City, then wherever the rock was hard and the pay in coin: Salt Creek's silver, three years now.
miner.work: Double-jack man and powder man at the silver mine; in town when he's off shift.
miner.place: A bed at the hotel; the bar of an afternoon, and its south end from seven.
miner.wants: Passage money for his wife Loveday and their girl, eleven years promised. He sends four pounds home most months.
miner.secret: The cough. It comes up black, he tells the doctor it's powder smoke, and he keeps it from the shift boss, who'd give his place to a younger man.

likes.why: Draws drill steel the way it should be drawn, and says nothing while he does it.
Asks after the cough and doesn't tell.
Keeps his bed when he's short.

dislikes.why: All that wind and never a day under ground.
A cheat, a dollar at a time; he sat in anyway, for the company.

miner.habit: Knocks twice on wood before he sits or drinks, as he'd sound a timber. Coughs into a blue rag and looks at it.
talks: Slow and heavy, a teacher's patience; 'my son' to any man, 'tis', 'it do', the surface is 'grass'.
A miner's word for everything: the drift, the face, timber, giant, bad air.
Never 'reckon' and never an oath stronger than 'damme'.
miner.voice: Fifties, deep, slow, West Cornwall under thirty years of America.
miner.clothes: Flannel shirt, canvas trousers, braces, heavy boots; candle grease on the hat; ore dust that never washes out.

lines.words: Same again, my son. It do lay the dust.
Ground's talking in the east drift. Only settling, timber man says, and him up to grass by ten every morning.
There's the whistle. Night shift coming up, and wanting the beds we're hardly out of.
Letter for St Just goes Thursday, missus. Four pound in it, if the cards leave me be.
'Tis only the powder smoke, Doctor. Comes up black of a morning and then I'm right.

fixed.talks: no_law.json's cast: 'a hard-rock man, slow and heavy, a little Cornish' (proposed there)

miner.notes: His one script line stands: 'He were cheating, my son, a dollar at a time, same as ever he did.' (no_law.json). 'He were' there is the script's wording (proposed there); the blind reader says Cornish runs 'they was', 'I be': to look at when that script is next read.
miner.in_town: Three years. He walked up alone from the end of the stage road in the spring of 'seventy-nine with his drills on his back, when the mine was one adit and a tent. He has seen it go to three shifts and a whistle, the hotel fill with its men, the cars come in 'eighty-one and bring cheaper men with them, and the Baron's fence posts go round water the mine's mules used to drink at. Before: tin at St Just from fourteen, copper on the Keweenaw, gold at Central City.

circle.friends: The south end of the bar with whoever is there; cards at Earl's table on a Friday, knowing what Earl is. He takes his drill steel down to Stroud himself, for the talk. Sits on the hotel's porch with Mrs. Rudd of an evening, neither saying much. Chapel-bred: he goes up to Hadley's church at Christmas and Easter and sings bass.
circle.family: His wife Loveday and their girl Tamsin in St Just; Tamsin is seventeen now, and he last saw her at six. A brother, Petherick, killed in the Keweenaw copper.

home.what: A bed in the back room of the hotel's upper floor, shared turn about with a night-shift man.

if_dies.grief: Mrs. Rudd strips the bed herself and won't let it that week. Stroud hangs his last set of drills on the smithy wall. Somebody has to write to St Just, and it's Mrs. Rudd who does.

lines.words: Jory Trembath, of St Just in Cornwall. Thirty-nine years under ground. He came to us twice a year and sang bass, and the rest of us couldn't be heard.
Fridays, he paid. Short, he'd come and tell me the night before, cap in his hand. His box is in my kitchen. I have the address off his letters.
Brung his own steel down, every time, and stood there and told me how it broke. I'll do his cross in iron.

if_dies.bearers: Stroud, Yount, Burdett, Mapes (who talks the whole way up), and two men off his shift.
if_dies.after: A younger man has his place on the shift by Monday. His stool at the south end stands empty a week, which costs the barkeep money and he allows it. Mrs. Rudd sends his box and his eleven dollars to St Just and adds to it from her own.

knows.what: Night one: he was at the bar. He saw Cody shoot Earl, and he saw a soft-spoken stranger hold a man in his chair at the next table. He stayed with Earl when the room emptied.
knows.tells: the doctor, as coroner, plainly; a deputy he respects
knows.takes: Trust. Ask him sober and away from the bar. He can give the stranger's hat, hands and voice; he doesn't know who he is.

knows.what: The mine: which drift talks, and where the timbering has been skimped.
knows.tells: any man who is going under ground
knows.takes: Nothing but being listened to. (Only if he is Buried Alive's miner: not decided.)

knows.what: The sawn floor: nothing.

miner.trouble: Nerve 0.6, nosy 0.5, duty 0.4. He doesn't run and he doesn't push forward: he moves off the line of it, slowly, puts his back to a post and watches. After, he is the one who goes to the man on the floor, as he would after a shot under ground. He'll carry a man. He won't take up a gun. At a fire he's worth three: he knows what a roof does before it comes down.

harlan.starts: Wary: a farmer with a badge.
harlan.warms: The sheriff's wound packed right; Earl carried to the doctor's door; a deputy who comes to the mine when men are under.
harlan.cools: A man who sat through Earl's killing and never spoke of it after; shooting a man with his hands up.

greets.warm: Deputy. Sit down, my son. I'll stand it.
greets.wary: Evening, Deputy. Quiet enough.
greets.afraid: I didn't see it, mister. I was looking in my glass.

jobs: The night-shift man who shares his bed has been gone three days with a fortnight's pay on him. Jory wants him found before the shift boss calls it desertion.
Somebody has been at the powder magazine's lock. He noticed; the shift boss doesn't want to hear it.
His letter with four pounds in it never reached St Just, and he thinks it never left the store.

looks.hair: Grey, cropped close by himself.
looks.beard: A grey chin-beard, the lip shaved.
looks.clothes: Flannel shirt, canvas trousers, braces, heavy boots; candle grease on the hat; ore dust that never washes out.
looks.wear: Ore dust in the creases of his neck and hands; candle grease on the hat; blue powder-marks under the skin of the left forearm.

casting.voice: Fifties, deep, slow, West Cornwall under thirty years of America.
casting.accent: West Cornwall, under thirty years of America.
casting.pace: Slow.

owns.money: About eleven dollars in a tobacco tin, and what the mine owes him till payday.
owns.home: A tin box under the bed: Loveday's letters, a Wesley hymn-book, a spare shirt, his own drills and a four-pound single jack.
owns.pockets: A blue rag, a clay pipe, three candle ends, matches in a tin.
owns.owes: Nothing on any slate: he won't drink on credit. Eleven years of passage money, to Loveday.

week.sunday: Sleeps late, mends, writes home with Mrs. Rudd's ink, one drink at dusk.
week.payday: Paid at the mine office at noon. The money order is put by before he lets himself into the saloon at six; cards after.
week.vices: Whiskey, steady, never drunk. Cards on Fridays. Not upstairs.

loyalty.why: The mine pays him and he doesn't love it. No dealings with the Baron: to Jory he is a farmer with a fence. He'd be against him the day he was shown who did what.

rancher.name: Anselmo Gallegos
rancher.called: Don Anselmo by those who know him; 'the Mexican' by those who don't
rancher.who: A New Mexican stockman whose family ran sheep on the creek before there was a town, and who sold the Baron his first meadow.
rancher.from: Abiquiú, New Mexico; north to the Conejos with his father's sheep in the fifties
rancher.came: Brought the flock over into this valley about 1860, when the grass was anybody's. He has been here longer than anyone in town.
rancher.work: Sheep and a few cattle on his place, eleven miles south. In town for the store and the livery of an afternoon, one drink at night.
rancher.place: The north end of the bar from a quarter past seven; his horse at the store's rail.
rancher.wants: To leave his sons a place with water on it and a paper the courts will read.
rancher.secret: He sold the Baron the low meadow in 1876, at a fair price. It was the Baron's first ground in the valley, and Anselmo counts it every winter.

likes.why: They speak Spanish together; his father traded with Joe's people.
The only other Catholic in town; they wait for the same priest twice a year.
Knows a horse.

dislikes.why: Called him 'the Mexican' across the room. Once.
He paid in full, and then the creek ran lower.

rancher.habit: Takes his hat off indoors and holds it. Stands at the bar; pays in coin, exact, before he drinks.
talks: English is his second language: courteous, complete, few contractions, 'with your permission'.
A Spanish word before the English one now and then ('acequia', 'compadre'), never for show.
Never swears in English. Says a hard thing as a courtesy.
rancher.voice: Fifties, low, a New Mexican's English: careful vowels, unhurried.
rancher.clothes: Short wool jacket, sash, wide flat-crowned hat, tall boots with big-rowelled spurs; everything old and brushed.

lines.words: One only, and I will take my time with it. The road home is dark past the ford.
My father watered sheep on that creek before there was a fence in this valley. Nobody asked him for a paper.
I sold him the low meadow in 'seventy-six. He paid what I asked, in gold, the same day.
Coffee. Two pounds of the Arbuckle's. You are writing it, Mr. Hollis? Good.
The left fore, Hiram. Look at it for me. He has said nothing, but he is... how is it. Favoring.

fixed.role: townsfolk brief §2, roster 13 (his face is the Studio's Mexican rancher)

rancher.notes: His father's water was never filed; nothing here gives him a right in the widow's ditch or changes the Baron's plan.
rancher.in_town: Twenty-two years in the valley, longer than the town. He came over from the Conejos about 1860 with his father, two brothers and eleven hundred sheep, when the nearest store was three days off. He saw the sheriff take up his claim in 'sixty-eight, the mine open, the street laid out on what had been his winter pasture, the cars come, and the Baron buy the valley a piece at a time, beginning with him. Before: his father's herder at Abiquiú.

circle.friends: He comes to town alone: the store and the livery of an afternoon, one drink standing at the north end of the bar. Spanish with Joe when they meet on the road, and with nobody else. Twice a year the priest comes through and says mass in Anselmo's front room, and Bérubé rides out for it.
circle.family: His wife Refugio, at the ranch. Sons Teófilo, thirty, who runs the sheep, and Eusebio, nineteen, who wants to go on the railroad. A daughter, Soledad, married at Conejos. His father and one brother are buried on the place.

home.what: An adobe house with a walled corral, eleven miles south.
home.where: off the valley's ground; only if a mission goes there

if_dies.grief: He is buried on his own ground, not on the town's hill, and Hadley has no part in it. The town learns of it from the black band on Teófilo's arm when he comes in for flour.

lines.words: He brought a horse in before it was lame. I ain't had ary other man do that. His boy can keep the stall, same price.
In this valley since 1860. I asked him the year twice, to have it right, and the second time he laughed at me. He is buried on his own ground; the priest comes in October.
He never owed me a cent past the first of the month. It's in the book. Twenty-two years... no. The book only goes back to 'seventy-four.

if_dies.bearers: His two sons, his brother and his herders. From town, Yount and Bérubé ride out.
if_dies.after: Teófilo has the place. Eusebio leaves for the railroad within the year. The Baron's man rides out inside a month with a figure for the south water, and nobody is left who remembers the valley before the fences.

knows.what: How the Baron buys: Anselmo was the first to sell (the low meadow, 1876). He can say what the offer sounded like, who carried it, and what the creek below did afterward.
knows.tells: the widow, without being asked, after the funeral; the deputy, if asked with respect
knows.takes: Courtesy and time. Not money: that would insult him.

knows.what: Night one: he was at the north end of the bar, and saw Cody and the stranger both. Coming in, he noticed a bald-faced sorrel at the rail, because he notices horses. He doesn't know whose it was.
knows.from: once the town has it that the sheriff's man rode a sorrel (after day two)
knows.tells: the deputy, and only if asked about the horse
knows.takes: Trust. PROPOSED, and Sean's to rule on: the bible has the sorrel at the rail that night and says nobody tells the player. This only lets a townsman confirm the horse later.

knows.what: The sawn floor: nothing.

rancher.trouble: Nerve 0.7, nosy 0.3, duty 0.5. He stands where he is, hat in his hand, until he knows who is shooting at whom; then he walks, not runs, to his horse. He doesn't gawk. Asked by name, he will help lift a hurt man and ride for the doctor. He carries an old cap-and-ball Colt on the road and leaves it with the barkeep in town: he would use it on his own ground, not in the street.

harlan.starts: Wary and courteous: another farmer with water the Baron wants, as he was.
harlan.warms: Looking to the widow; treating Joe as a man; an arrest where a shooting was easier.
harlan.cools: Taking the Baron's side or his money; letting Joe hang.

greets.warm: Deputy. A glass. Sit, sit.
greets.wary: Good evening, Deputy.
greets.cold: Señor. I am only buying flour.
greets.afraid: No, no. I am going. My horse is there.

jobs: Forty of his sheep are dead along the Baron's south fence, their throats cut. He wants it written down by the law, not avenged.
His younger son has taken wages from the Baron's foreman to wrangle horses. Anselmo asks the deputy to see what kind of work it is.
A survey party has driven stakes across his ditch, and he can't read what is painted on them.

looks.hair: Grey going white, to the collar.
looks.beard: A grey moustache; the chin shaved.
looks.clothes: Short wool jacket, sash, wide flat-crowned hat, tall boots with big-rowelled spurs; everything old and brushed.
looks.wear: Brushed dust, the smell of wool, a hat sweat-stained and kept in shape.

casting.voice: Fifties, low, a New Mexican's English: careful vowels, unhurried.
casting.accent: A northern New Mexican's English, Spanish first.
casting.pace: Slow, with a stop now and then to find the word.

owns.money: More than anyone guesses: the Baron's gold for the meadow is still in a chest, less what one bad winter took. About nine hundred sheep.
owns.home: The adobe, a saint in a niche, his father's saddle.
owns.pockets: A rosary, a clasp knife, tobacco and corn husks, the exact coin for one drink.
owns.owes: Nothing. A wool buyer at Pueblo owes him.

week.sunday: Prayers at home, read by Refugio. He doesn't come to town.
week.payday: He stays away from town on a payday: too many strangers.
week.vices: One glass. A husk cigarette. No cards, nothing upstairs.

loyalty.side: against him, and silent about it
loyalty.why: He sold to the Baron once and won't again. He is afraid for his sons, not for himself.

earl.name: Earl
earl.called: Earl. Nobody can give his other name.
earl.who: The card player Cody kills on night one, in front of the whole saloon.
earl.work: Cards, at the saloon's table from half past seven.
earl.place: The west chair of the card table; in from Back Street. After night one, the undertaker's.
earl.secret: He cheats, a dollar at a time, and the table knows it.
earl.habit: Leaves the dime for a drink the barkeep meant to stand him.
talks: Caught out and placating; quick to smile, quicker to apologise.

lines.words: Now, Cody, I never...
Mind my arm.

fixed.name: the bible (Earl); the undertaker's line: 'Nobody can give me his other name'
fixed.secret: the miner's script line, and Cody's

earl.notes: Where he's from and what he wanted are open, and his other name stays unknown: the undertaker's book says so.

if_dies.grief: He does die, on night one. The barkeep is out four dollars. Kitty minds, and says so only to the fiddler.

lines.words: Earl. Nobody can give me his other name. Shot by one Cody, before witnesses. Pine box, charged to the county.
He owes me four dollars.
Earl. That is all of his name we have, and Mr. Colby has asked. He played cards in this town longer than anyone can tell me.
Cheated me a dollar a time, three year, and I knowed it. Friday I'd have sat in, same as always.

if_dies.bearers: The barkeep, Trembath, Burdett, Yount.
if_dies.after: The west chair is empty, and the game goes on with three.

drifter.name: Wiley Burdett
drifter.who: A Texas hand between jobs who forks hay for a loft to sleep in and sits across the card table from Earl.
drifter.came: Up the trail to Dodge with a herd in 'seventy-nine, then Tascosa, then wherever the talk said there was work. The talk was wrong about Salt Creek too.
drifter.work: Odd jobs. Forks the livery's stalls at six for his bed; holds up the saloon's porch post till supper.
drifter.place: The livery's loft, on credit; the card table's east chair at night.
drifter.wants: A riding job, forty a month and found. He'd take one tomorrow.
drifter.secret: He sold his saddle in Tascosa to eat, and tells it as stolen. A hand without a saddle is nobody's hand, and he knows the Baron's outfit hires men who needn't rope.

likes.why: Grumbles and feeds him.
Talks to him though she knows what's in his pocket.

dislikes.why: Keeps offering him two dollars a day to swing a hammer.
He has ridden with that kind and got out of it once.

drifter.habit: Leans on whatever is nearest. Rolls a cigarette and puts it behind his ear for later.
talks: Dry and low, slow East Texas; a joke said without a smile.
Counts in miles and months' pay; 'I'm out' is most of his card talk.
Never complains straight: he says what a thing costs.
drifter.voice: Twenties, low and unhurried, East Texas.
drifter.clothes: Faded shirt, a hand's boots worn over at the heel, spurs he still wears and no horse; hay in his hat brim.

lines.words: Forty forkfuls buys me the loft. I counted.
Saddle? Stole, in Tascosa. Ask me about something else.
Deal me in light. I got a dollar and it's to see me to Sunday.
Baron's outfit's hiring. Sixty a month, and they don't ask can you rope.
Your deal, Earl. Cut 'em where I can see.

drifter.notes: Built and script lines that stand: 'I'm out.', 'Rode in from Tascosa. Nothing there either.', 'Just holding up the wall. It'd fall without me.' The town script's brief says twenties; No Law's says thirties.
drifter.in_town: Since the spring. He rode in alone on a borrowed horse, which has gone back to its owner. He is too new to have seen anything change; what he knows of the town he has from Yount. Before: up the trail to Dodge in 'seventy-nine, a winter riding line in the Panhandle, Tascosa.

circle.friends: Yount, whose stalls he forks. Kitty, on the saloon's porch at the lamps' hour. The card table with Earl when he has a dollar, its edge when he hasn't. Sundays he walks out to the creek and sleeps.
circle.family: A mother and three sisters in Angelina County; he writes at Christmas. A brother, Asa, went up the trail in 'seventy-seven and wasn't heard of again.

home.what: The livery's loft, on credit, worked off at forty forkfuls a morning.

if_dies.grief: Yount pays for the box and says the county did. Kitty keeps the cigarette from behind his ear.

lines.words: Wiley Burdett. Mr. Yount gave me the name, and Texas, and that is as far as anyone here can take it.
Forked clean. Never asked me for nothing but the loft. Texas is all he'd say, and I didn't push him.
He'd roll one and put it behind his ear and never smoke it. I've it here.

if_dies.bearers: Yount, Stroud, Mapes, and Peck, who was asked because he was standing there.
if_dies.after: The loft is empty. Yount forks his own stalls at five and is short with everybody for a month. Bérubé writes to the postmaster at Homer, Texas.

knows.what: Night one: he was in the east chair, across from Earl, nearer than anyone. He heard every word and saw Cody's face. He saw the stranger sit down at the next table before any of it began.
knows.tells: nobody, at first: he wants no part of it. The deputy, later.
knows.takes: A meal, and being asked at the livery, not in the saloon. A threat works too (nerve 0.4), and then he tells the next man who threatens him as well.

knows.what: The Baron's hiring: sixty a month for men who needn't rope, offered on the saloon's porch; and which of the men standing about took it.
knows.tells: Yount; the deputy
knows.takes: Trust.

knows.what: The sawn floor: nothing.

drifter.trouble: Nerve 0.4, nosy 0.6, duty 0.2. He is out of his chair and behind something at the first raised voice, and then he watches from the door: he has seen enough of it to know when. He fetches nobody unless he is told to by name. The one thing he runs toward is a fire at the livery: he would have the horses out before anyone asked.

harlan.starts: Wary: the law has moved him on from three towns.
harlan.warms: Not being moved on; a meal stood him; Yount treated right.
harlan.cools: Being asked where his saddle went; a man taken up for having no work.

greets.warm: Deputy. You want that horse walked, I ain't busy.
greets.wary: Deputy. Just leaning.
greets.cold: I ain't done nothing but stand here.
greets.afraid: I'm going. Loft's got a back ladder.

jobs: He wants his saddle back. He says it was stolen in Tascosa, and he has seen it since on a horse at the Railroad Saloon's rail. The pawn ticket in his pocket says otherwise.
A man by the stock pens offered him five dollars to hold four horses after dark and ask nothing.
Yount is short a horse he hired out on Tuesday, and won't go to the law about it himself.

looks.hair: Sandy, sun-bleached, wanting a cut.
looks.beard: Three days' stubble; never a beard.
looks.clothes: Faded shirt, a hand's boots worn over at the heel, spurs he still wears and no horse; hay in his hat brim.
looks.wear: Hay in the hat brim, boot heels run over, a paler band on his hip where a holster used to hang.

casting.voice: Twenties, low and unhurried, East Texas.
casting.pace: Slow and low.

owns.money: A dollar and some cents.
owns.home: A blanket; a war bag with a spare shirt, a razor and his brother's one letter; a bridle and no horse.
owns.pockets: The makings, a clasp knife, a pawn ticket from Tascosa.
owns.owes: Yount, three weeks of loft, being worked off. The barkeep, sixty cents. Earl, two dollars.

week.sunday: The creek. Sleeps, and washes his shirt.
week.payday: Stands at the card table's edge hoping a winner stakes him; holds drunk miners' horses at a dime.
week.vices: Cards when he has a dollar. Tobacco. Whatever is stood him.

loyalty.side: for hire, and not hired yet
loyalty.why: The Baron's sixty a month tempts him and he hasn't taken it. He would by winter if nothing else turned up. What stops him is Yount, and having watched Cody work.

fiddler.name: Lemuel Stiles
fiddler.who: An old Arkansas fiddler who has played for dances since before the war and plays the saloon by ear.
fiddler.from: Izard County, Arkansas, in the White River hills
fiddler.came: Lost the farm after the war and followed the railroad camps west, a dollar a night and supper. Stopped where the camp did.
fiddler.work: Fiddle at the saloon from seven; on the dance hall's stage with the band on a payday night.
fiddler.place: By the saloon's upright; a cot over the saloon.
fiddler.wants: To play out the nights he has left sitting down, and be asked for the old tunes.
fiddler.secret: His left hand is stiffening. He soaks it in warm water at the bar before he plays, and he has started to leave out the high part of 'Leather Britches'.

likes.why: Thirty years younger and can't play without paper; Lem wouldn't play with anyone else.
She calls the tunes for him when the room won't.

dislikes.why: Docks him for the nights the room empties early.

fiddler.habit: Tunes with the fiddle against his jaw and his eyes shut. Keeps time with his left heel.
talks: Little, and old-fashioned: 'I allow', 'a right smart', 'I'd as lief'.
Names the tune and where he learned it; nothing about himself.
Rode with an Arkansas regiment and doesn't bring it up.
fiddler.voice: Sixty, thin and cracked, Ozark hills.
fiddler.clothes: A black coat gone green at the seams, collarless shirt, a rosin smudge on the left shoulder.

lines.words: Well, call it. 'Soldier's Joy'? I allow I can still find 'Soldier's Joy'.
You go on and read it off the paper, Professor. I'll be along by ear.
Warm water, in a bowl. It ain't to drink. It's for the hand.
That's 'Leather Britches'. Had it off my uncle, on the White River. He had it off somebody.

fiddler.notes: The roster sleeps him at the hotel; valley_folk.json has his home as the saloon. This sheet follows the game's data.
fiddler.in_town: Two years and some. He came in with the graders' camp in 'eighty on a supply wagon, the fiddle in a flour sack, and when the camp moved on up the grade he didn't. He has seen the tents on Main Street become fronts, the saloon get its upright and then its Professor, and the cars come. Before: corn in Izard County; four years in an Arkansas infantry regiment; ten years of dances and railroad camps across Kansas and the Territory.

circle.friends: Vogel: they don't talk, they play. Kitty, who calls the tunes. Afternoons he sits on the saloon's back step in the sun with his left hand in a bowl of warm water.
circle.family: His wife Sarah died in 'sixty-eight. A son, Lemuel, somewhere in Texas, not written to in nine years. A married daughter at Batesville, who gets two dollars at Christmas.

home.what: A cot in the lumber room over the saloon.

if_dies.grief: The room has no fiddle. Vogel plays 'Leather Britches' alone, slow, without paper, for the first time.

lines.words: He never came in on the beat, not once. I wrote some of his tunes down. Eleven. He had, I don't know. Two hundred.
Lemuel Stiles, of Arkansas, sixty years old. He played this town's dancing every night it danced, and Saturdays till one, which I have heard about from my bed.
I docked him for slow nights. I did, I'll say it. That fiddle's his daughter's, I guess, if anybody knows what town she's in.

if_dies.bearers: Vogel, the barkeep, Yount, Stroud, Mapes, Trembath.
if_dies.after: The piano plays alone until the payday band. Kitty asks for 'The Rose of Tralee' and nobody can play it by ear. The barkeep sends to Durango for a fiddler and learns what one costs.

knows.what: Night one: he was by the piano, facing the room, and saw all of it. The stranger sat down before it began.
knows.tells: nobody who doesn't ask
knows.takes: Trust: sit down and ask for a tune first. He is deaf on the right side since the war, and has heard less of the room's talk than men suppose.

knows.what: The sawn floor: on Payday afternoon he is on the dance hall's stage, tuning. If anyone felt that floor give before the night, it was him.
knows.tells: the barkeep, who wouldn't listen; the deputy
knows.takes: Only if the story wants a trace beforehand (SETUPS.md S23): PROPOSED.

fiddler.trouble: Nerve 0.4, nosy 0.5, duty 0.2. He stops on the note, holds the fiddle to his chest and steps behind the upright: the instrument first. He has been shot at by regiments and doesn't lose his head. He won't help and he won't fetch. Afterward he plays, quietly, because somebody ought to.

harlan.starts: Wary, without a grudge: he can tell a Union soldier by the way he stands.
harlan.warms: A tune asked for; trouble stopped in the room before it starts.
harlan.cools: Shooting in the saloon; soldiers brought to town.

greets.warm: Deputy. Name it and I'll play it.
greets.wary: Evening.
greets.afraid: Ain't no call for that. I'm an old man with a fiddle.

jobs: His bow is gone from the top of the piano. He thinks a drunk section hand took it for a joke.
He wants a letter got to a son in Texas, and doesn't know the town.
The barkeep docked him three nights. He wants somebody with a badge to say that ain't right.

looks.hair: White, thin, long over the collar.
looks.beard: White stubble; a moustache stained with tobacco.
looks.clothes: A black coat gone green at the seams, collarless shirt, a rosin smudge on the left shoulder.
looks.wear: Rosin on the left shoulder; the knuckles of the left hand swollen.

casting.voice: Sixty, thin and cracked, Ozark hills.
casting.pace: Slow; a crack in it.

owns.money: Six dollars in a sock.
owns.home: His grandfather's fiddle, its case lined with a piece of army blanket; a cot; a bowl.
owns.pockets: Rosin, a spare E string, a jew's harp, a plug of tobacco.
owns.owes: The barkeep, for whiskey, taken out of his dollar a night.

week.sunday: Sleeps, and sits in the sun. He doesn't play on a Sunday: Sarah's rule.
week.payday: The dance hall's stage with the band, till the floor quits.
week.vices: Whiskey, a little and all day. Chewing tobacco.

loyalty.why: He plays for whoever is in the room, the Baron's riders included. They tip.

pianist.name: Augustus Vogel
pianist.called: the Professor; 'Gus' to nobody but the fiddler
pianist.who: A Cincinnati church organist come down to a saloon upright, who stops playing and gets under it when trouble starts.
pianist.from: Cincinnati, Ohio, a German cabinet-maker's son from Over-the-Rhine
pianist.came: Played the variety houses in Leadville until a man was shot against the piano he was playing. He took the next stage out, and Salt Creek was where his money stopped.
pianist.work: Piano at the saloon from seven till one; the stage's upright on a payday night.
pianist.place: The saloon's piano stool; a room over the saloon.
pianist.wants: A church with an organ and a salary, and Mrs. Rudd's good opinion.
pianist.secret: He is sweet on the landlady and thinks nobody knows. The saloon woman tells everybody.

likes.why: She keeps a parlor organ and lets him mend it.
Has never once come in on the beat, and is never wrong.

dislikes.why: Leans on the piano with his gun side.
Won't pay a tuner.

pianist.habit: Wipes the keys with a handkerchief before he sits. At a raised voice his hands stop first, and then he looks.
talks: Fussy and proper, a town man's English, 'if you please'; his father's German shows only when he's rattled.
Complains of the instrument and the damp, never of people.
Never swears. 'Ach' escapes him.
pianist.voice: Forties, soft, precise; Cincinnati with his father's German behind it.
pianist.clothes: A clean collar every night, striped vest, sleeve garters, coat hung on the piano's end.

lines.words: The C above middle sticks. It's stuck since the wet weather. I told him, and he asked me what a new one costs.
Gentlemen, the glass doesn't go on the instrument. On the floor, if you please.
That was a chair. Was that a chair? I'll just get down here till somebody tells me.
The parlor organ only wants a reed, Mrs. Rudd. I could look at it Sunday. It's no trouble.
In Leadville the house had a Steinway. A man was shot against it, and they had me play it the same night, wet.

fixed.role: townsfolk brief §2, roster 10; #276: he stops when trouble starts, ducks, and starts again shakily
fixed.secret: town.json: 'The piano man's sweet on the landlady. Don't say I told you.'

pianist.notes: Sunday is the one day he could go up to the hotel by daylight; his day in the game is nights only, so his hotel line waits for a Sunday block.
pianist.in_town: A year. He came in on the cars from Leadville in the autumn of 'eighty-one with a valise of sheet music and forty dollars; the barkeep had just freighted in an upright and had nobody to play it. He has seen the dance hall go up and the Baron's riders get louder. Before: organist at a German church in Cincinnati, a music teacher, three years in Leadville's variety houses.

circle.friends: Stiles, at the piano. Mrs. Rudd, on Sundays, over her parlor organ. He buys paper collars and peppermints from Mrs. Hollis. He would like to play the church's harmonium and has never dared ask a Methodist.
circle.family: His mother and a sister, Ottilie, in Cincinnati, who believe he teaches at a conservatory in Denver.

home.what: A room over the saloon.

if_dies.grief: Mrs. Rudd shuts the lid of the parlor organ and doesn't have it mended.

lines.words: Professor could play anything you set in front of him, off the paper. I'd learn him the 'Arkansaw Traveler' by ear and he'd write it down after, every note, and play it wrong.
Mr. Vogel mended my organ and ate in my kitchen for it. He should have had the dining room.
Augustus Vogel. He asked me once at the store, very low, what hymn-book we use. I told him the Methodist, and he nodded as though that settled something, and went back across the street.

if_dies.bearers: The barkeep, Yount, Stroud, Peck, Burdett and the undertaker's hired man. Stiles walks behind.
if_dies.after: The piano is shut, and the C still sticks. A letter comes from Ottilie addressed to a conservatory.

knows.what: Night one: he stopped on the shout and went under the piano, and from there he saw boots. He can say which way the stranger's went afterward, and that they didn't hurry.
knows.tells: Mrs. Rudd, who tells the street; the deputy, if he isn't asked in the saloon
knows.takes: Gentleness. A threat makes him say anything, true or not.

knows.what: Which of the Baron's riders have new money: he watches the bar over the top of the piano all night.
knows.tells: Stiles
knows.takes: Trust.

knows.what: The sawn floor: on Payday night he is at the stage's upright, and would feel a floor through the pedals.
knows.takes: Only if the story wants a trace (S23): PROPOSED.

pianist.trouble: Nerve 0.2, nosy 0.5, duty 0.2. His hands stop, there are two wrong notes, and he is under the keyboard (Sean, #276). He stays there until somebody tells him. He starts again thin and a little fast. He never helps and never looks, and afterward he is sick in the yard. At a fire he would go back for the sheet music and have to be pulled out.

harlan.starts: Wary, as of any armed man.
harlan.warms: Guns kept out of the saloon; a word of thanks for the music.
harlan.cools: A pistol drawn in the room, whatever the cause.

greets.warm: Deputy! Guten Abend. Good evening. You want something played?
greets.wary: Good evening, Deputy.
greets.afraid: Bitte. Not in here. Not by the piano.

jobs: Somebody in Leadville has been writing to him about a faro debt of ninety dollars, and now writes that he is coming in person.
The takings box under the piano's lid is eight dollars light, and the barkeep thinks it was him.
A reed for Mrs. Rudd's organ, ordered from Chicago, was signed for at the depot by somebody who wasn't him.

looks.hair: Brown, thinning, combed across with pomade.
looks.clothes: A clean collar every night, striped vest, sleeve garters, coat hung on the piano's end.
looks.wear: Soft white hands; ink on the right cuff from copying music.

casting.voice: Forties, soft, precise; Cincinnati with his father's German behind it.
casting.accent: Cincinnati; his father's German in the rhythm when he's rattled.
casting.pace: Quick, soft, fussy.
casting.say_name: aw-GUS-tus VO-gel (he says FO-gel; nobody else does)

owns.money: Twenty-two dollars in his music case.
owns.home: The valise, a dozen collars, a metronome, a picture of his mother.
owns.pockets: A handkerchief, a tuning fork, peppermints.
owns.owes: Ninety dollars at faro, in Leadville.

week.sunday: He walks up Church Lane as far as the gate and hears the hymn from outside; then the hotel's organ. His best day.
week.payday: The stage's upright till the floor quits. Three dollars, and he hates it.
week.vices: None now. Faro was the vice, in Leadville. Peppermints.

loyalty.why: He is afraid of every armed man, and the Baron's are the most of them. No dealings.

doctor.who: The town's one doctor, an educated man gone west; as coroner he is the acting sheriff once the sheriff dies, and keeps Harlan on.
doctor.work: His dispensary and front room; crosses the street to a call and back.
doctor.place: The doctor's; sleeps behind the dispensary.
doctor.wants: To get back to his patient.
doctor.secret: He knows more about the sheriff's wound than he says. What he keeps back is open in the bible.

likes.why: The only other man in town who writes a thing down exactly.
The boy boils what he's told to boil.

doctor.habit: Counts: hours, beds, pints. Washes his hands before and after, which is his own habit and not the profession's.
talks: Brisk, whole sentences, no slang, dry.
The medicine of 1882: the ball, lint, carbolic, laudanum, shock.
Never says all he knows, and never raises his voice. 'I can do nothing', not 'I'm sorry'.
doctor.voice: Late forties, an educated Easterner; brisk, quiet, dry.

lines.words: Somebody packed that wound, and packed it right. That's bought him some hours. Come back tonight.
Bring them in if you like. I never yet saw a white man hang on an Indian's word.
Morning. If you're bleeding, come by. If you're not, good.
That cough of yours wants listening to. Come by.

fixed.name: roles only (C14 c)
fixed.from: open in the bible ('from where: O')
fixed.habit: VOICES.md ('Counts things'); WORDS.md ('clean is his own habit')
fixed.knows: VOICES.md, The doctor, 'Knows' (B1, B3, B5, B12); what he keeps back is O (s19)
fixed.harlan.starts: VOICES.md, The doctor, 'Calls Harlan'; C12 a (coroner, acting sheriff, keeps Harlan on)
fixed.home: config/valley.json (the doctor's lot); valley_folk.json (sleeps behind the dispensary)
fixed.casting: the scripts' cast (voice); C14 c (no name)

doctor.notes: Only his two likes are proposed here. His cough line to the miner is the town script's; the miner's secret is written to it. #1311: every other new section is PROPOSED (marked where it touches what the bible leaves open: where he's from, his family, his dials, his looks); the sheet's own `from`, `came`, `body` and `clothes` stay null until Sean fills them.
doctor.in_town: PROPOSED: four years; he came in 'seventy-eight, by stage, with a medical school's diploma, two trunks of books and a microscope, after a practice in the East that he doesn't speak of. Where from stays open (the bible's O). He has seen the mine's accidents go from one a month to one a week, the cars bring a druggist's catalogue, and the town's dead come to his front room first. Before: medical school and a city hospital's wards (where, open).

circle.friends: Colby, the only other man in town who writes a thing down exactly. Caleb, whom he pays and teaches. Mrs. Rudd, at whose table he eats at noon. He plays chess by himself and reads the journals a month late.
circle.family: Open in the bible. PROPOSED: none he speaks of; a letter comes twice a year from a woman in Philadelphia and he answers it the same day.

home.what: The room behind the dispensary, a bed and his books; the front room is for the sick and the dead.

if_dies.grief: There's no doctor for two days' ride. The county has no coroner. Caleb sits on the dispensary's step. Mrs. Rudd sets his place at noon and takes it up again.

lines.words: He sat up with the sheriff to the end, and with half of you before that. I never knew him send a bill to a widow.
Three hundred and some certificates he wrote me. I have them filed by the year, the cause on one line, every one.
I scrubbed in the carbolic this morning, to the elbow, like he showed me, and then I stood there with my hands up.
Asked after my chest every time he passed, he did. Not a word of it to the shift boss, my son, not ever.

if_dies.bearers: Colby's hired man, Trembath, Yount, Hollis, Bérubé, Caleb; Stroud to the gate.
if_dies.after: Nobody signs the certificates: Colby writes 'cause unknown' for the first time. Until the county names a man, the deputy holds the badge on nobody's word now. The next man shot is carried to Pueblo in a wagon and dies on the road.

knows.what: From B1: that the sheriff will die, and that whoever packed the wound has done it before (built).
knows.tells: the deputy
knows.takes: Nothing: he says it.

knows.what: From B3: the sheriff's last words; from then he is acting sheriff, and the deputy holds the badge on his word.
knows.tells: the deputy; the inquest, as coroner
knows.takes: Nothing.

knows.what: From B5: what was done at the camp (Joe is in his office). That the law won't punish it.
knows.tells: the deputy
knows.takes: Nothing.

knows.what: From B12: that he can't take them all, and what Rourke's paper is for.
knows.tells: the deputy
knows.takes: Nothing.

knows.what: What he keeps back about the sheriff's wound: open in the bible (s19). Not written here.

doctor.trouble: PROPOSED: nerve 0.8, nosy 0.3, duty 1.0. He crosses the street to a call with his bag, whatever is going on in it. He doesn't take cover until there's a man on the ground, and then he takes it beside the man. He doesn't carry a gun.

harlan.starts: From the bible: he keeps the deputy on, and calls him 'Harlan' in private and 'Deputy' in front of the town (after B3).
harlan.warms: A wound packed right; a man brought in alive; doing what he's told and not asking why.
harlan.cools: Men killed who might have been brought in; drink before a call; a man brought in dead who had given himself up.

greets.warm: Deputy. Sit. I have ten minutes before the Swede's dressing wants changing.
greets.wary: Deputy. Is somebody hurt?
greets.cold: If it's not a wound it can wait, Deputy.
greets.afraid: Put that down. I have a man on the table.

jobs: Laudanum gone from the dispensary, two ounces, measured. He has his idea who and won't say it aloud.
A miner with a crushed hand won't come in, because the shift boss would see. The doctor wants him carried down.
As coroner he needs six men for an inquest jury by noon and the saloon won't lend him any.

looks.hair: PROPOSED: dark, greying, cut short.
looks.beard: PROPOSED: a close-trimmed dark beard going grey at the chin.
looks.clothes: PROPOSED: a dark frock coat off for work, a waistcoat, shirt sleeves rolled, a black bag.
looks.wear: Hands scrubbed raw; carbolic; ink on the right cuff.

casting.voice: Late forties, an educated Easterner; brisk, quiet, dry.
casting.pace: Brisk; whole sentences; counts.

owns.money: PROPOSED: what the county pays the coroner, late; forty dollars; a book of bills he doesn't send.
owns.home: His instruments, a microscope, the journals, a medicine chest, the front room's table.
owns.pockets: A watch, a lancet case, a stub of pencil, a list of the day's calls.
owns.owes: The druggist in Denver. Nobody in town.

week.sunday: PROPOSED: no church. Calls at the ranches in the buggy, and the journals.
week.payday: He keeps the lamp lit till two for the stitching.
week.vices: PROPOSED: a glass of claret at supper; sleep he doesn't get.

loyalty.why: As coroner he is the law until the county names a man, and he keeps the deputy on. What he thinks of the Baron he doesn't say until it can be proved.

storekeeper.name: Amos Pratt Hollis
storekeeper.called: Mr. Hollis; 'Amos' to his wife and the livery man
storekeeper.who: Keeps the general store and half the valley's debts, every one of them in the book.
storekeeper.came: His store at Boonville was cleaned out twice in the war, once by each side. He sold what was left and came out behind the mines in 'seventy-four, to a place nobody had fought over yet.
storekeeper.work: The store, seven to half past five; sweeps his walk at six; a drink with the livery man till half past nine.
storekeeper.place: The general store, A. P. HOLLIS in gilt on the windows; lives over it.
storekeeper.wants: The book paid down before the railroad brings a second store.
storekeeper.secret: Night riders. He has stood behind a counter while armed men helped themselves, and he bars the door at dark and sells to anybody by day, the Baron's men included.

likes.why: The one man he drinks with; they argue about the railroad every night and neither moves.
Pays in coin and never asks the price twice.

dislikes.why: Carries his freight and drinks the pay before it's earned.
Stands in front of the store all day and buys a collar.

storekeeper.habit: Says the sum aloud, writes it, and says it again. Wets the pencil.
talks: Careful, polite to the penny; a Missouri 'I reckon' and 'directly'.
Says less when he's frightened, not more.
Never guesses: 'it's in the book'.
storekeeper.voice: Fifties, a Missouri man, dry and careful.
storekeeper.clothes: Apron, sleeve garters, a pencil behind the ear, spectacles pushed up.

lines.words: Four dollars and ten cents. I'll say it again when I've wrote it, so we both heard.
I reckon it'll be on Thursday's cars. Directly it's here I'll send the boy round.
The bar goes across that door at dark. I don't open for a knock, and I don't care whose.
Hiram, about that lamp oil. No, drink your drink. Saturday'll do.
Better than a thousand dollars on that book, and not forty in the drawer.

fixed.name: Sean, #1067: A. P. Hollis, gilded on the windows (what A. P. stands for is proposed)
fixed.talks: VOICES.md, Smaller voices: 'Careful; everything's written down'

storekeeper.notes: The bible's line stands: 'One handsaw, to a man I never saw before. It's in the book. Everything's in the book.' One of the Colters is called Hollis too (a first name); no kin.
storekeeper.in_town: Eight years. He came up from the Arkansas in the fall of 'seventy-four with Lavinia and two wagons of stock, when the mine was a prospect hole and a promise, and put up the first front on the street; his book starts that October. He has seen the smithy and the saloon go up beside him, the hotel, the mine's three shifts, the cars come in 'eighty-one with a Denver drummer on every one, and the Baron's account grow to the biggest on his book. Before: a store at Boonville, cleaned out once by Price's men and once by the militia.

circle.friends: Yount, every night at the saloon's back table till half past nine, the same argument about the railroad. Sundays he sits at the back of Hadley's church and counts the plate in his head. He keeps out of the bar's front, and he's never sat at Earl's table.
circle.family: Lavinia. Their daughter Susan, married to a railroad clerk in Pueblo, with a boy he has seen once. A brother in Boonville who writes at Christmas and wants money.

home.what: Three rooms over the store: a parlor with Lavinia's piano that nobody plays, the kitchen, the bedroom over the street. The bar for the door leans by the stairs.

if_dies.grief: Lavinia shuts the store one day and opens it the next, with the book on the counter where it always is. Yount doesn't come in to the saloon that night, or for a week.

lines.words: Mr. Hollis put up the first front on this street. There are men standing here whose winter he carried on his book, and he wouldn't tell me which, though I asked him.
Every night, him and me. He'd say the cars was the making of us and I'd say they'd ruin us, and then he'd be at his purse before I could get to mine.
He wrote it all down, every sack of flour since 'seventy-four. I have the book upstairs, and I don't intend that any of you should lose sleep over it this winter.

if_dies.bearers: Yount, Stroud (to the gate), Peck, Bérubé, Gallegos, and Mapes, who still swears he was shorted two loads.
if_dies.after: Lavinia keeps the store open, and the debts stop being collected. The Denver house sends a man to look at the stock. By spring there's talk of a second store by the depot, which is the thing he was afraid of.

knows.what: Night one: nothing he saw. He had barred the door at dark, the sheriff being shot, and heard it from upstairs with Lavinia's hand on his arm.
knows.tells: anyone, as the reason he bars the door
knows.takes: Nothing.

knows.what: The handsaw (SETUPS.md S23): on the morning of Payday Night he sold one handsaw, fine-toothed, to a man he had never seen before, and wrote it in the day-book on the counter. He thinks nothing of it: men buy saws. 'One handsaw, to a man I never saw before. It's in the book. Everything's in the book.'
knows.from: Payday Night, the morning (the saw is bought before anyone knows how the train will go)
knows.tells: a man who asks him about strangers, or reads the book on the counter; he volunteers it to nobody
knows.takes: The right question. Before the floor he can give the man's coat and that he paid in silver, not what he wanted it for. After the floor (B12) he says it to the deputy unasked, once he has heard there was a cut.

knows.what: The Baron's account: the biggest on the book, settled each quarter in gold by the foreman; cartridges by the case since spring, more than a ranch shoots at coyotes.
knows.tells: nobody: it's business
knows.takes: Being shown why it matters, by a man he trusts, with the door shut. A threat gets nothing: he says less when he's frightened.

knows.what: The sawn floor: only the saw, as above.

storekeeper.trouble: Nerve 0.3, nosy 0.4, duty 0.5. At a shot he has the bar across the door before the echo stops, and Lavinia behind the counter with him. He doesn't look out. When it's over he opens up, puts lint, carbolic and a bolt of sheeting on the counter for whoever comes, and writes each one down for the county. At a fire next door he is on the roof with wet sacks, because the store is everything he has.

harlan.starts: Wary: a deputy brings trouble to a man's door, and a man with a badge has been known to help himself.
harlan.warms: Paying on the nail; the store robbery stopped (store-robbery); being asked about the book and not told what to think of it.
harlan.cools: Shooting in the street near his windows; the Baron's riders made angry at the town; anything taken from the shelf for 'the law' without a word written.

greets.warm: Deputy. Your cartridges are on the counter, wrote down. Saturday'll do.
greets.wary: Deputy. Something I can sell you?
greets.afraid: Whatever you want. Take it.

jobs: Mapes swears the store shorted him two loads' pay. Hollis wants the deputy to read the book and tell Mapes so, in front of the bench.
Somebody tried the bar on the back door at two in the morning. Nothing taken. He hasn't slept since.
A box of .44s is short on the shelf and the book says it was never sold. He'd as soon not know who, if it was one of the Baron's men.

looks.hair: Thin, sandy going grey, combed flat with water.
looks.clothes: Apron, sleeve garters, a pencil behind the ear, spectacles pushed up.
looks.wear: Pencil lead on the right fingers; flour on the apron; a stoop from the counter.

casting.voice: Fifties, a Missouri man, dry and careful.
casting.pace: Careful; slower with numbers, and slower still when he's frightened.

owns.money: Under forty dollars in the drawer; better than a thousand on the book; four hundred in the bank at the county seat.
owns.home: The store and its stock, the rooms upstairs, a Hall's safe, Lavinia's piano, the day-books back to 1874 in a crate.
owns.pockets: A pencil, a short rule, the keys, a Missouri half-dime for luck.
owns.owes: The Denver wholesale house, six hundred on ninety days. The bank's note on the building.

week.sunday: Church with Lavinia, at the back. The store shut; the books in the afternoon.
week.payday: The best day on the book and the worst for his nerves: the mine's men pay down, the store open till dark, the bar across at dark all the same.
week.vices: One drink a night with Yount, two on payday. Worry.

loyalty.why: The Baron's is the biggest account on the book and the foreman pays in gold. He sells to his men and asks nothing, as he sold to both sides in the war. He would never stand against him in daylight; with the book, he might in court.

store_wife.name: Lavinia Hollis
store_wife.who: Runs the store's dry goods and the valley's mail, and knows from what people buy what is happening to them.
store_wife.from: Boonville, Missouri; taught school there before she married
store_wife.came: With Amos in 'seventy-four. Their one daughter married a railroad clerk and lives in Pueblo.
store_wife.work: The dry-goods side and the mail; two hours a day on the store's bench.
store_wife.place: The general store and its bench; lives over it.
store_wife.wants: A school in Salt Creek, and to be asked to teach it.
store_wife.secret: She reads the smith his sister's letters and writes his answers, in the back of the store with the door shut, and has never told a soul he can't.

likes.why: He listens to a letter the way other men listen to a sermon.
He prints the children's compositions, and she is the one who collects them.
She is most of his congregation.

dislikes.why: The other end of the street always has the news first.
'Those women'; she sells to her and looks at the shelf while she does it.

store_wife.habit: Reads a postmark before she hands a letter over. Corrects a child's grammar and gives him the candy anyway.
talks: Plain and brisk, a schoolteacher's grammar; 'I'll thank you to' is a warning.
Longer sentences than the landlady's: tells what she knows as a thing she happened to notice.
Never an oath; never a man's first name but her husband's.
store_wife.voice: Forties, clear and quick, Missouri with the schoolroom over it.
store_wife.clothes: Dark calico, a white collar, an apron with scissors on a ribbon.

lines.words: Black crape, two yards. That's the third time this year I've cut it, and it isn't harvest yet.
There's a letter come for the smith. Tell him it's here, and tell him I have the time this afternoon.
Mr. Peck was in again. A paper collar. That makes one a week since March, and never so much as a spool of thread with it.
She pays cash, that girl. I will say that for her, and I'll thank you not to repeat it.
Amos, the man asked for lamp wick, not what you think of the railroad.

store_wife.notes: Her pool in the town's script is `townswoman`.
store_wife.in_town: Eight years, with Amos, in 'seventy-four. She has seen the street go from their one front to two rows, the mail come up by stage and then by the cars, and the town get children enough for a school and no school. She has seen 'those women' arrive, and the church built. Before: taught the district school at Boonville from seventeen until she married.

circle.friends: Hadley, whose congregation she mostly is: she brings three wives on Sundays and starts the hymn when he loses it. Bérubé, who prints the children's compositions she collects on Fridays. Stroud, in the back of the store with the door shut and a letter. The wives of the bakery and the butcher, on the store's bench in the mornings.
circle.family: Amos. Their daughter Susan in Pueblo, who writes every Sunday. A sister in St. Louis who married better and says so.

home.what: The rooms over the store.

if_dies.grief: Amos stands behind the counter and can't make the sums come. The mail goes unsorted for a week. Stroud stops coming in.

lines.words: Mrs. Hollis brought me four of my nine the first Sunday, and the hymn-books in a basket. When I lost the tune she'd start it again from the second row, and I'd follow her.
She'd read one twice if I asked. Never looked up at me, doing it. There's one come from my sister Tuesday, and it ain't opened.
Twenty-five years. I'd wet the pencil, and she'd already— She did the sums. I wrote them.
The compositions came Fridays, in her basket, the spelling corrected in red. This week's came Thursday. I do not know how to print red.

if_dies.bearers: Yount, Stroud (to the gate), Bérubé, Peck, the doctor, and the baker.
if_dies.after: Nobody reads the smith his letters. The children's compositions stop. Amos sells the piano. Mrs. Rudd has the news first now, and finds she doesn't want it.

knows.what: The valley's mail: whose letters come from where, who sends money and who stopped. Kitty's money orders to Pueblo, eight dollars on the first: she sells them, and has never said a word.
knows.tells: nobody, of Kitty; of the rest, the deputy, as things she happened to notice
knows.takes: Trust, and a good reason. She is ashamed of reading postmarks and does it anyway.

knows.what: The ranch's mail: letters in Army envelopes, from department headquarters, all spring. Beef contracts, she supposes; the Army buys beef. PROPOSED, for Sean: an innocent notice that means something only after B12 (the letter's date) and B14 (the papers); it gives nothing away alone.
knows.tells: the deputy, if he asks what comes for the ranch
knows.takes: Being asked plainly. She'd think it was nothing.

knows.what: Night one: nothing. She was upstairs with Amos and the door barred.
The sawn floor: nothing.

store_wife.trouble: Nerve 0.5, nosy 0.7, duty 0.6. At a shot she calls the children in off the walk by name, all of them, hers or not, and shuts them in the back of the store. Then she watches from the upstairs window and can tell you the order it happened in. After, she is on the street with the store's sheeting and the doctor's name. In a brawl she says 'I'll thank you to stop that' once, and has been obeyed.

harlan.starts: Warm, with a schoolteacher's reserve: the sheriff was a reader.
harlan.warms: Being civil to Kitty in front of the store; the children walking past the saloon safe on a Saturday; a man who reads.
harlan.cools: Swearing in front of the bench; drink on him in the store; anyone killed in front of a child.

greets.warm: Good morning, Deputy. Nothing for you in the mail, I'm afraid. Coffee's on in the back.
greets.wary: Deputy. I'll thank you to wipe your boots.
greets.afraid: My husband is just upstairs. He'll be down directly.

jobs: A letter came to the store with its seal lifted and stuck down again. Not her doing, and she wants to know whose before Amos hears of it.
She wants every child in the valley counted for the county, to show there are enough for a school. The ranches won't answer her; they might answer a deputy.
The Gallegos boy and the butcher's boy fought at the creek, and the butcher's wife says a knife came out. Lavinia doesn't believe it and wants it looked into before it's believed.

looks.hair: Brown with grey at the temples, parted in the middle and drawn back in a knot.
looks.clothes: Dark calico, a white collar, an apron with scissors on a ribbon.
looks.wear: Ink on the second finger; spectacles on a cord, put on to read a postmark.

casting.voice: Forties, clear and quick, Missouri with the schoolroom over it.
casting.accent: Missouri, schooled out of it but for the vowels.
casting.pace: Quick and even; longer sentences than anyone on the street.

owns.money: Egg money and the dry-goods side's takings in a tea caddy: thirty dollars, hers.
owns.home: Her school books, a McGuffey set for the school that isn't, the parlor piano, a copy of Mrs. Beeton.
owns.pockets: Scissors on a ribbon, spectacles, a peppermint for whichever child has earned it.
owns.owes: Nothing. Stroud thinks he owes her, and she won't let him.

week.sunday: Church, three wives brought with her; she starts the hymns. Writes to Susan in the afternoon.
week.payday: The mail is heaviest the day after: money orders home, by the dozen. She sells them and keeps her face still.
week.vices: Reading other people's postmarks. Sugar in her tea.

loyalty.why: She has watched what his riders buy and how they talk on the bench, and the sheriff was a friend. She would say so before Amos would, and Amos knows it.

liveryman.name: Hiram Yount
liveryman.who: Keeps the livery, counts feed in nickels, and grumbles to hide that he minds.
liveryman.came: Drove a six-mule team for the Army's quartermaster through the war and freighted the Santa Fe road after it, till the railroad took the road. He bought the livery with what the mules fetched.
liveryman.work: The livery from five in the morning; first up in the street, the last lamp out but the saloon's.
liveryman.place: The livery; sleeps in its harness room.
liveryman.wants: To see every horse in his barn go out sound and come back the same.
liveryman.secret: His eyes are going. At dusk he knows a horse by running a hand down it, and he is afraid of the day somebody notices which stall he walked past.

likes.why: Thirty years of the same argument with different men; this one's the best at it.
The boy forks clean and doesn't ask for anything. He'd not say so.
Brings a horse in before it's lame, not after.

dislikes.why: Four shoes owing, and he is reminded of it by everyone but the smith.
An ox driver. Whips what he can't talk to.

liveryman.habit: Runs his hand down a horse's near foreleg before he says a word to its rider.
talks: Grumbles; every kindness comes out as a complaint about what it costs.
Kentucky: 'ary' for any; horses are 'he' and men are 'that fellow'.
Never says a horse is fine. He says what's wrong with it.
liveryman.clothes: Collarless shirt, braces, a leather apron for the feet, chaff on everything, an old Army teamster's hat.

lines.words: Come round his near side. He can't see you on the off.
Oats is two cents a pound now. Two cents. And that bay'd eat the manger if I let him.
You sleep up there on my say. Fork the far stalls first, they been standing in it.
Cars'll run clear to the mine by spring, Amos. Then who hires a team? You tell me.
Four shoes I owe the smith for. He ain't said ary word about it. I wish he would.

fixed.talks: VOICES.md, Smaller voices: 'Grumbling to hide that he minds'

liveryman.notes: The bible's line stands, for after the funeral: 'That horse is eating my oats, and the man that owned him's in the ground. Somebody ought to take him home to her.' The roster sleeps him in the loft and the drifter there too; here the loft is the drifter's and the harness room his.
liveryman.in_town: Two years. He came up on the last of the freight before the cars, in the summer of 'eighty, with eight mules to sell and a bad eye coming on, and bought the livery off a man going to Leadville. The Army's quartermaster through the war; the Santa Fe road after it, twelve years. He's seen the cars take the freighting, Hollis pay Mapes by the load and then stop, and the Baron's riders stable at the ranch and not with him.

circle.friends: Hollis at the saloon's back table every night till half past nine. Sarge, to argue mules with on the livery's bench of an afternoon: they have it out every day. Burdett, who forks his stalls. Gallegos, who knows a horse. He doesn't go to church and says the preacher's horse is a disgrace.
circle.family: Nobody living that he speaks of. A wife who died in Kansas City in 'sixty-eight, of the cholera. A nephew in Covington who writes when he wants a loan.

home.what: A cot in the harness room, with the stove and the lantern and the ledger he can't read well by now.

if_dies.grief: Burdett forks the stalls the next morning without being told. The horses aren't fed till late the first day, and the town hears them.

lines.words: Mr. Yount had a corner of near every box that's come up this hill since he came, and all he ever said on the way was to mind the ruts.
He'd say the far stalls was a disgrace. Then he'd go do 'em himself before I was up, and tell folks I had.
I went over at half past nine last night, out of habit. The lamp was out in the harness room. I stood at the door a while before I come home.
He said a mule can count to four. I said three. Well, I'll not get that settled now.

if_dies.bearers: Hollis, Burdett, Stroud (to the gate), Trembath, Gallegos, Sarge (sober).
if_dies.after: The livery shuts until a nephew sells it to the Baron's man, who doesn't keep it as a livery. Burdett has no loft. Hollis drinks alone at half past nine, and then stops going.

knows.what: Every horse that stables in town and whose. The sheriff's horse, from day 2, eating his oats (the widow's place opens from it: 'Somebody ought to take him home to her').
knows.tells: anyone at the livery door, as a complaint about oats
knows.takes: Nothing.

knows.what: The ranch's riders never stable with him; their horses stand at the saloon's rail. He didn't see the stranger's horse on night one and wouldn't know it.
knows.tells: the deputy
knows.takes: Asking.

knows.what: His eyes: he walks past a stall at dusk and can't say what's in it. Nobody knows.
knows.tells: nobody
knows.takes: Catching him at it.

knows.what: The sawn floor: nothing.

liveryman.trouble: Nerve 0.5, nosy 0.3, duty 0.6. At a shot he shuts the barn's doors and stands inside them with a fork. At a fire anywhere on the street he has the horses out first, a sack over each one's eyes, cursing the whole time: then he comes to the buckets. He doesn't gawk and doesn't fetch. He'd use the fork.

harlan.starts: Wary: the sheriff's horse is in his barn and nobody's paid for it.
harlan.warms: Taking the sheriff's horse home to the widow (widows-place); bringing a horse back sound; paying for the stall without being asked.
harlan.cools: A horse run lame; the ranch's men given the street; the drifter moved on.

greets.warm: Bring that one round. I'll look at the near fore. Ain't charging you for looking.
greets.wary: Deputy. Stall's a quarter. Feed's extra.
greets.afraid: Take the bay. Take him. Only don't run him on the road, he ain't— Go on, take him.

jobs: The sheriff's horse eats his oats, and the man that owned him's in the ground: somebody ought to take him home to her (the bible's; it opens widows-place).
He's short a horse he hired out Tuesday to a man who said Pueblo. He won't go to the law about it himself; he'll grumble at the deputy until the deputy goes.
His horses are sweated in the mornings. Somebody rides them at night and puts them back.

looks.hair: Grey, thick, cut by Mrs. Rudd at the kitchen door twice a year.
looks.beard: A grey spade beard stained by tobacco.
looks.clothes: Collarless shirt, braces, a leather apron for the feet, chaff on everything, an old Army teamster's hat.
looks.wear: Chaff; the smell of the barn; a cloudy left eye he turns away.

casting.voice: Fifties, gravel, northern Kentucky.
casting.accent: Northern Kentucky (the Ohio river), thirty years on the road.
casting.pace: Steady, grumbling; quick only when he's afraid.

owns.money: Sixty dollars in a coffee tin in the harness room, and what the town owes for stalls.
owns.home: The livery and its lot, nine horses and two mules, harness, a buggy for hire; his Army discharge in the ledger.
owns.pockets: A hoof pick, a twist of tobacco, a horse's tooth he won't explain.
owns.owes: Stroud, four shoes; he'd pay if the smith would say. The bank, the last of the livery's price.

week.sunday: The horses, same as any day. The bench in the afternoon with Sarge, and a mule to argue over.
week.payday: Every horse hired out by noon and two come back lame by night.
week.vices: His one drink with Hollis, and chewing tobacco.

loyalty.why: The ranch's riders never pay him a stall and ride their horses hard. He'd no more work for the Baron than for the railroad. He fears him less than he should.

smith.name: Eben Stroud
smith.who: The blacksmith at the west end: at his fire before anyone is up, proud of his iron, and no hand with a pen.
smith.from: A charcoal-furnace town in Lawrence County, Ohio
smith.came: Bound to the furnace's smith at twelve; shod horses for an Ohio cavalry regiment through the war; came out dressing tools for the railroad's graders and stayed for the mine's drill steel.
smith.work: The smithy from five: shoes, wagon tires, and sixty drills a day off the mine to be drawn and tempered.
smith.place: The smithy at the west end; lives behind it.
smith.wants: A striker he can teach the trade to, at two dollars a day. He has his eye on the drifter's shoulders.
smith.secret: He can't read. He signs with his touchmark, a struck S, and Mrs. Hollis reads him his sister's letters.

likes.why: She reads a letter twice if he asks, and never looks at him while she does.
Brings his own steel down and tells him exactly how it broke.

dislikes.why: A man with clean hands who wants to sell him a lot.

smith.habit: Looks at the colour of the iron, never at the man talking. Hands a bill back for the other man to read out.
talks: Slow and few; iron, heat and money owed.
Says a price once. 'I'll make my mark' for signing.
Never talks about the war, and never says what he thinks of a man.
smith.voice: Forties, big and slow-spoken, southern Ohio.
smith.clothes: Leather apron scorched at the hem, sleeves cut off, soot to the elbows, a cloth cap.

lines.words: That's drill steel off the mine. Sixty a day, and they dull 'em faster than I can draw 'em.
You read it out. I'll make my mark on it after.
Cherry red, see. Go on to white and it's burnt, and you pay for the iron twice.
You got the shoulders for a striker. Two dollars a day. You'd have to turn up.
I won't be up the hill for it. Hinges for the box is mine, tell him. No charge.

fixed.role: townsfolk brief §2, roster 6; he doesn't walk to the funeral (brief §3)
fixed.secret: town.json's cast: 'proud of his iron, shy of his letters' (#1184)

smith.notes: His town-script lines stand ('Livery owes me for four shoes. Don't tell him I said.').
