Why he carries a box to the gate and no further: the burial detail at Stones River, which he never talks about. Nobody in town knows it; the first nine list him as a bearer, and his card squares it: he takes his corner to the foot of Church Lane and hands it to whoever is behind.
smith.in_town: Two years. He came up the line with the railroad's graders in 'eighty, dressing their picks, and when they went on he bought the smithy off a Swede who'd had it since 'seventy-six and wanted to go home. He's seen the mine's work turn his shop to drill steel, sixty a day, and the cars bring bar iron cheaper than it ever came by wagon.

circle.friends: Trembath, who brings his steel down himself. Mrs. Hollis, who reads him his letters. Caleb Rudd on the bellows when he can get away. He drinks at the bar on payday, a short beer, and is home by eight.
circle.family: His sister Ruth in Ironton, Ohio, who writes every other month and thinks he answers in his own hand. A wife and a boy who died of the diphtheria at the furnace in 'sixty-six, when he was not long home from the war.

home.what: A room behind the smithy, against the forge wall for the warmth, with a bed and a chest.
home.where: the blacksmith's lot at the west end (not built yet)

if_dies.grief: The smithy's fire goes out for the first time in two years, and the street notices the quiet before it notices why. Trembath takes the drill steel to the mine's own forge, and swears at it.

lines.words: He made most of the iron crosses on this hill, and charged nobody. He'd carry a man as far as that gate and give his corner to whoever was behind him.
His sister in Ohio is called Ruth. She writes every other month, and I have answered for him these two years in a hand she must take for his. Now I have to write to her in mine.
Four shoes. I owe him four shoes. Who do I pay now? You tell me that.
He'd let me on the bellows. Said I'd make a striker if I could quit talking.

if_dies.bearers: Trembath, Yount, Burdett, Caleb, and two men off the mine; they carry him through the gate he never came through.
if_dies.after: No smith in town: shoes and tires go to the mine's forge, which charges double, and the drill steel goes dull. There's no iron for the next cross, and the next grave on the hill has a board.

knows.what: Iron: a broken shoe, a sprung tire, a drawn spike. PROPOSED, for Sean: after Hell on Wheels, shown one of the pulled rail's spikes, he can say it was drawn with a claw bar, not shaken loose by the train. It only confirms what the player already holds (K7 is learned at B11).
knows.from: after Hell on Wheels, if shown a spike
knows.tells: whoever brings it to him
knows.takes: Bringing it to the smithy. He won't go and look.

knows.what: Night one: nothing. He was asleep behind the forge by eight.
The sawn floor: nothing.

smith.trouble: Nerve 0.8, nosy 0.2, duty 0.5. A shot down the street doesn't stop his hammer. A brawl at his door, he picks a man up by his belt and sets him in the road. At a fire he's first with the buckets and a hook to pull down what's burning. He has his hammer in his hand already and doesn't need a gun; he'd never take one up.

harlan.starts: Wary, the way he is with everyone: he looks at the iron.
harlan.warms: Paying for a shoe without reading the bill; reading him a paper without being asked to; never mentioning it after.
harlan.cools: Being made to sign a thing he can't read; a man who brings trouble to the smithy.

greets.warm: Deputy. Hold that a minute. No, by the tongs.
greets.wary: Shoe or a tire?
greets.afraid: I ain't got nothing against you. Put it down.

jobs: The mine's shift boss pays for fifty drills a day and sends sixty. Stroud won't argue it with a man who can write; he'd like the deputy to count them.
Somebody took his sledge from the smithy door. It has his mark on the face, a struck S.
A rider left a horse to be shod and never came back for it, and the bill's three weeks old.

looks.hair: Black, cropped short against the sparks.
looks.beard: A short black beard with a burn-scar bald through it.
looks.clothes: Leather apron scorched at the hem, sleeves cut off, soot to the elbows, a cloth cap.
looks.wear: Soot to the elbows; small white burn-scars on both forearms; one ear thick from a horse.

casting.voice: Forties, big and slow-spoken, southern Ohio.
casting.accent: Southern Ohio (the Hanging Rock iron country), half Kentucky.
casting.pace: Slow and few.

owns.money: A hundred and twenty dollars in a can buried under the forge's floor.
owns.home: The smithy, its anvil and tools, a chest with his cavalry jacket and Ruth's letters in it.
owns.pockets: A piece of chalk, a nail, his touchmark punch.
owns.owes: Nothing. Yount owes him four shoes and he won't say.

week.sunday: The fire banked. He mends his own tools and sits at the smithy door. He doesn't go up to church.
week.payday: The mine pays his contract at noon. A short beer, one, at the bar, home by eight.
week.vices: None to speak of. He chews.

loyalty.why: He shoes the ranch's horses for cash and the foreman pays without looking at the bill. He has no opinion of the Baron that he would say aloud, which is the only kind of opinion he has.

landlady.name: Hester Rudd
landlady.called: Mrs. Rudd (Mrs. Cornelius Rudd, on paper)
landlady.who: A widow who runs the hotel, feeds the mine's men, and knows who is behind with his board.
landlady.from: Lockport, New York, where her mother kept boarders on the canal
landlady.came: Her husband Cornelius built the hotel in 'seventy-seven to board the mine's men, and died of lung fever in its second winter. She kept it open the day of the burying.
landlady.work: The hotel: the rug over the porch rail at six, three meals, the beds; an hour on the porch at dusk.
landlady.wants: The note on the hotel paid, and her boy Caleb in a trade that isn't the mine.
landlady.secret: Cornelius's boots still stand by the kitchen door, blacked, so a caller thinks there is a man in the house.

likes.why: Twenty years her husband's kind of man; she keeps his bed when he's short.
Her son.
Pays the boy and teaches him to wash.

dislikes.why: Three weeks behind and a clean collar on.
Has an opinion of the hotel's sheets.

landlady.habit: Shakes the rug as if it owed her money. Counts heads at table before she sits.
talks: Brisk and plain, never loud; a New Yorker's 'I guess'.
Says the rule and the hour, once, and a man's name first.
Never asks a man his business; she tells him what she has noticed.
landlady.voice: Forties, level, upstate New York; never raised.
landlady.clothes: Grey wool, a long apron, sleeves pinned back, keys at the waist.

lines.words: Supper's at six. Six. I don't hold a plate.
Mr. Peck. Three weeks, I guess you know. I'll have something on it by Saturday.
Twenty-six beds, and the mine sends me men who never slept in one.
You may look at the organ, Mr. Vogel. Supper's in the kitchen for it.
Caleb. The doctor's wood box first. Then the slops.

fixed.talks: town.json's cast: 'a widow who runs the hotel; brisk, plain, has fed worse men than these. Never raises her voice'

landlady.notes: Her town-script lines stand ('Your room's paid to Friday. After that, we'll see.' is to Mr. Peck's kind).
landlady.in_town: Five years. She came out from Lockport with Cornelius and Caleb in 'seventy-seven when Cornelius took the hotel's contract, and buried him in its second winter, of lung fever, in 1879. She has seen the mine's men fill her beds twice over, the cars bring drummers who want sheets changed, and Mr. Peck. Before: her mother's boarding house on the canal at Lockport, from a girl.

circle.friends: Trembath on the porch of an evening, neither saying much. Vogel over her parlor organ, Sundays. The doctor, who pays Caleb and teaches him to wash. She leaves a plate on the back step for Sarge at half past six and has never mentioned it to a soul. She doesn't go to the Hollises' and they don't come to her.
circle.family: Caleb, sixteen. Cornelius on the hill under an iron cross Stroud didn't make (it was before him). A married sister in Rochester.

home.what: Her room off the hotel's kitchen, with Cornelius's boots by the door.

if_dies.grief: Caleb sits in the kitchen and won't eat. The mine's men find there's no breakfast and go to the saloon for it. The plate isn't on the back step at half past six.

lines.words: She kept the hotel open the day we buried Cornelius. The men who carried him came down the hill and she had their dinner on at noon.
Six o'clock. I was late most nights. She'd say my name the once, at the door, and that'd do it.
Kept my bed when I was short, she did, and never a word of it in front of the table. 'Tis her I wrote home about, more than the mine.
Half after six there'd be a plate on the back step with a cloth over it. Biscuits, Tuesdays. I'd like to know who told her I was partial to biscuits.

if_dies.bearers: Trembath, Yount, Stroud (to the gate), Peck, Vogel, the doctor. Caleb walks behind and won't be given a corner.
if_dies.after: The hotel's note is called. Caleb goes to his aunt in Rochester or the doctor keeps him: the town takes sides on which. The mine's men are in the saloon's back room at night, and there are more fights.

knows.what: Who's in her beds, who's behind, and who left in the night. Every stranger who takes a room in Salt Creek signs her book.
knows.tells: the deputy, if he asks at the right hour (after dinner, before supper)
knows.takes: Asking her plainly, once. She tells what she noticed, not what she thinks.

knows.what: PROPOSED, for Sean (one possible answer to s22, how the deputy knows the men on the gallery): on the morning of Payday Night two men took her front rooms for a week, paid in advance, in gold, and asked for the gallery side. They were out all that night. She thought nothing of it until the floor.
knows.tells: the deputy, the day after, if he asks about strangers
knows.takes: Trust; she won't have shooting in her house, and says so.

knows.what: Night one: nothing she saw. Trembath came back late and sat in her kitchen and said a man was dead; she gave him tea.
The sawn floor: nothing.

landlady.trouble: Nerve 0.7, nosy 0.6, duty 0.7. At a shot she locks the front door, sends the guests into the kitchen, and tells Caleb to stay where he is, which he never does. She puts water on to boil before anyone asks for it. A brawl in her dining room, she takes the coffee pot to it. She doesn't run and she doesn't watch.

harlan.starts: Wary: Caleb talks about him too much.
harlan.warms: Sending Caleb home instead of along; paying for a meal; keeping the shooting off her porch.
harlan.cools: Caleb taken into danger; a fight brought into the hotel; Peck put out on the street.

greets.warm: Deputy. There's a plate kept back. Kitchen.
greets.wary: Deputy. Dinner's at noon. Boots off the rail.
greets.afraid: Caleb, go up. Now. ... Well? What is it you want?

jobs: A drummer left in the night without paying, and his valise was full of bricks. She wants the bricks' price.
Mr. Peck is three weeks behind. She won't put him out. She'd like the deputy to say a word to him so she needn't.
Caleb is at the depot at all hours. She asks the deputy to bring him home, and not to tell him she asked.

looks.hair: Dark, greying, scraped back under a cap.
looks.clothes: Grey wool, a long apron, sleeves pinned back, keys at the waist.
looks.wear: Red, cracked hands from the wash; flour at the hem.

casting.voice: Forties, level, upstate New York; never raised.
casting.pace: Brisk; short sentences; the hour and the rule.

owns.money: The board money in a cash box in her room, sixty-odd dollars a week in and most of it out again.
owns.home: The hotel, on a note to the Denver bank; twenty-six beds; the parlor organ; Cornelius's boots.
owns.pockets: The keys, a pencil, a list.
owns.owes: The bank, the hotel's note, due each quarter. Hollis, for flour, paid every Saturday.

week.sunday: Breakfast at seven, dinner at one, no supper but cold. Vogel at the organ in the afternoon. Church once a month, when she can leave the kitchen.
week.payday: Board collected from the mine's men at the door before they reach the saloon.
week.vices: None. A sherry at Christmas.

loyalty.why: She takes any man's board who pays. The Baron's riders drink on her gallery and she charges them for the chairs. Against him, if she were shown why; she would want to be shown.

churchman.name: Enoch Hadley
churchman.who: A Methodist circuit man with a church at the top of the lane and nine people in it, who walks Main Street every morning to be seen.
churchman.came: Twenty years on horseback round the Kansas circuits; the Conference gave him Salt Creek when his knees gave out, a mining town nobody else asked for.
churchman.work: The church up Church Lane; one walk down Main Street and back, eight to nine; the buryings.
churchman.place: The church (north-west, up the lane) and the house beside it.
churchman.wants: A full bench on a Sunday, and a second stove before winter.
churchman.secret: The north side of his roof is the Baron's shingles. He thanks him by name every Sunday, and has begun to wonder what he was bought for.

likes.why: She sings, she brings three others, and she tells him who is sick.
Does his part properly and bills the county, not the widow.

dislikes.why: Eleven shutters to his one.

churchman.habit: Lifts his hat to every soul, the saloon woman included. Walks with a stick and stops to count things.
talks: Plain and carrying; the old words at a grave and his own in the street.
Asks; doesn't preach outside his own door.
Never an oath, and never 'damnation' on a weekday.
churchman.voice: Fifties, a carrying voice, plain, Indiana; reads the old words without performing them.
churchman.clothes: Black coat shiny at the elbows, a white stock, a wide black hat, a blackthorn stick.

lines.words: Nine on Sunday, Mr. Hollis, and four of them came in with your wife. Tell her I said so.
I don't ask what's in the glass. I ask are you coming Sunday. There's a stove.
Eleven shutters on that saloon. I have the one on the church, and it wants a hinge.
North side of that roof is the Baron's shingles. I thank him for them by name, every Sunday, out loud.
Hymn-books is eight. Sing off your neighbor's.
Man that is born of a woman hath but a short time to live, and is full of misery. He cometh up, and is cut down, like a flower.

fixed.talks: no_law.json's cast: 'a Methodist circuit man; carrying voice, plain, unadorned'

churchman.notes: Two roster ids, one man: `churchman` walks the street by day, `preacher` is the funeral's act man (aliases).
churchman.in_town: Two years. The Conference sent him in the spring of 'eighty, when his knees gave out on the Kansas circuits, to a church the miners had framed and nobody had preached in. Mapes carried the stove up the hill for him on his own back and took nothing for it. He has seen the congregation go from four to nine, the saloon add shutters, and the Baron's shingles go on the north side of his roof. Before: twenty years on horseback through Kansas, three hundred miles a round.

circle.friends: Mrs. Hollis, who brings three of the nine and tells him who is sick. Colby, at every burying. He stops on his walk for anybody: Sarge on the church's low step on Sundays (he leaves the door open on his side), Kitty on the saloon porch (he lifts his hat). He takes his supper at the hotel on Wednesdays.
circle.family: His wife Martha, buried at Council Grove in 'seventy-three. Two grown sons in Indiana, one a Methodist preacher and one who isn't anything, and writes more.

home.what: Two rooms in the house beside the church, a cot, his books, a stove that smokes.
home.where: beside the church, up Church Lane (the church stands; the house is not built yet)

if_dies.grief: There's nobody to bury him: the Conference is three weeks away by letter. Mrs. Hollis reads the service from his own book. The nine come, and more than nine.

lines.words: There's no one to read it, so I shall. He'd marked the place himself, in his own book, with a slip of paper. I only found it this morning.
Left the door propped my side, Sundays. I'd sit on the low step and get the hymn for nothing.
Six foot and one half inch. He asked me for his measure in 'eighty and I gave it him, and he said, 'Then that's settled.'
I carried that stove up this hill on my back for him. Took nothing for it. Nothing! You ask anybody.

if_dies.bearers: Colby, Hollis, Mapes, Yount, Trembath, Peck; Stroud to the gate. Sarge walks behind, sober.
if_dies.after: The church stands shut until the Conference sends a younger man who doesn't walk the street. The door isn't open on Sarge's side. The Baron sends a letter of sympathy, and Mrs. Hollis doesn't read it out.

knows.what: The Baron's shingles: given the spring before last, when the roof leaked on the bench. He thanks him every Sunday and has begun to wonder what for.
knows.tells: anyone who asks about the roof
knows.takes: Nothing.

knows.what: PROPOSED, for Sean: last winter the Baron asked him, idly, at the church door, whether the sheriff's wife had any people back East the place might go to. Hadley thought it a kindness. After B4 (the grave, the water named) he understands the question.
knows.tells: the deputy, in the church, not in the street
knows.takes: Being asked in the church. He would think it a confidence otherwise.

knows.what: Who is sick, who drinks, who stopped coming: the street's whole state of health, from Mrs. Hollis.
knows.tells: the deputy, as a thing to pray for
knows.takes: Walking with him.

knows.what: The sawn floor: nothing.

churchman.trouble: Nerve 0.6, nosy 0.5, duty 0.9. He walks toward it, slowly, with his hat on and his stick, which has stopped one fight in his life. He kneels by the man on the ground whoever shot him. He doesn't run, doesn't take up a gun, and doesn't get out of the way when he should.

harlan.starts: Warm: the sheriff came to church at Christmas, and swore him in.
harlan.warms: Coming up the hill on a Sunday; a burying done decently; Sarge let alone.
harlan.cools: A man shot in the back, or with his hands up; drink on him at a grave; the Baron's account believed against his own people.

greets.warm: Good morning to you, Deputy. Walk with me as far as the corner, if you're going that way.
greets.wary: Morning, Deputy. Mind the mud by the trough.
greets.cold: I had heard. Good day to you.
greets.afraid: You'll put that up, now. Whatever it is. There's a woman at that window.

jobs: The church's poor box was broken open Saturday night. Four dollars and a Mexican real. He doesn't want the man punished, he wants him found and fed.
Sarge has back pension owing as First Sergeant Tolliver and won't sign for it (his card). Hadley asks the deputy to write to the Pension Office.
Men come out of the saloon at midnight and sing under his window, the same three songs. He wants the deputy to ask them for a fourth.

looks.hair: White, long at the back, thin on top.
looks.beard: A white chin-beard, the upper lip shaved.
looks.clothes: Black coat shiny at the elbows, a white stock, a wide black hat, a blackthorn stick.
looks.wear: Saddle-bowed legs, a stiff walk from the knees; mud on the stick's ferrule.

casting.voice: Fifties, a carrying voice, plain, Indiana; reads the old words without performing them.
casting.pace: Unhurried, carrying; slower at a grave.

owns.money: The Conference's three hundred a year, of which he has seen two hundred; nine dollars in a drawer.
owns.home: The church's Bible and his own; Wesley's sermons; a bed, a stove, a horse he doesn't ride.
owns.pockets: A New Testament, a pencil, a list of the sick.
owns.owes: Hollis, for lamp oil and the hymn-books. The Baron, he has begun to think.

week.sunday: Preaches at ten and at six. Stands at the door to shake every hand, and lifts his hat to Sarge on the step.
week.payday: Walks past the saloon twice in the evening, slowly, so the men see him.
week.vices: Coffee, strong. He lets a sermon run long.

loyalty.why: The Baron's shingles are on the roof, and he thanks him for them by name. He'd turn the day he understood what the shingles were for, and say so from the pulpit.

saloon_girl.name: Catherine Dolan
saloon_girl.who: Works the saloon's room at night: quick, tired, and able to tell a man's pay from the way he comes through the door.
saloon_girl.came: Burned out in the Fire at thirteen and in service at fourteen; Denver by nineteen, where the wages for a girl in a kitchen were three dollars a week. The barkeep pays a share of every drink she sells.
saloon_girl.work: The saloon from seven: bar to tables, a dollar for a glass of cold tea, sits with whoever is winning.
saloon_girl.place: A room over the saloon; its porch for the lamps' hour.
saloon_girl.wants: Four hundred dollars and a hat shop in a town where nobody has seen her before.
saloon_girl.secret: A little girl, Nora, four years old, boarded with a carpenter's wife in Pueblo. Eight dollars goes by money order on the first of every month.

likes.why: Never put a hand on her, and tipped his hat as if she were the minister's wife.
Plays 'The Rose of Tralee' when the room's thin, without being asked.
Broke, and knows it, and doesn't pretend.

dislikes.why: Pays and thinks that settles it.
Takes her money looking at the shelf.

saloon_girl.habit: Looks at a man's boots, then his hands, then his face. Laughs with her mouth before her eyes.
talks: Quick and teasing, tired underneath; says the price first.
Chicago Irish: 'himself' for the barkeep; reads a man by his boots.
Never tells a man her other name, and never says 'love'.
saloon_girl.voice: Twenties, quick, a little hoarse; Chicago with her mother's Cork in the vowels.
saloon_girl.clothes: The red dress with the hem mended twice, a shawl for the porch, hair up with two combs.

lines.words: Buy a lady a drink? It's cold tea and it's four bits, and himself gets three of them.
That one's off the section gang. He'll have been paid Thursday. Look at his boots, they're new.
He's had six and he's showing me a picture of his mother. I want paying for that.
Hold eight back for the first, same as always. Money order, Pueblo.
Earl'd tip his hat to me. On the stairs, in front of them all. Like I was the minister's wife.

fixed.role: townsfolk brief §2, roster 16; DESIGN.md §5: 'people, not prizes'

saloon_girl.notes: 'The girls' to the barkeep, 'those women' to the town (WORDS.md); she is nobody's joke. Her town-script lines stand.
saloon_girl.in_town: Two years. She came down from Denver on the stage in 'eighty with another girl, Mae, who left with a drummer the first winter. She has seen the saloon double, the cars bring section hands and drummers, and the Baron's riders come in since spring with more money and worse manners. Before: Chicago, in service at fourteen; Denver.

circle.friends: Stiles, who plays what she asks. Burdett, on the porch at the lamps' hour. The two other women upstairs (not on the roster yet). The barkeep is business. Sunday afternoons she walks out to the creek alone.
circle.family: Her daughter Nora, four, boarded at Pueblo. A brother, Dan, a hod carrier in Chicago. Her parents are dead.

home.what: A room over the saloon.

if_dies.grief: The barkeep pays for a proper box and a stone, and is surprised at himself. The money orders to Pueblo stop, and nobody knows whom to write to unless somebody reads the stubs.

lines.words: Catherine Dolan, twenty-four. That was her name, whatever the street called her. I lifted my hat to her on that porch most mornings, and she'd nod back, the way a lady does.
She never shorted the till. Jesus. Eight dollars the first of every month to Pueblo, and I never asked her what for. Who's got them stubs?
She'd call the tune when the room wouldn't. I'll play her the Rose. I allow I can get through it.
She paid cash. I never looked at her when I took it.

if_dies.bearers: The barkeep, Burdett, Yount, Stroud, Trembath. The town's wives don't walk up, but Mrs. Rudd does.
if_dies.after: The saloon's porch is empty at the lamps' hour. A woman in Pueblo writes in pencil to 'the saloon, Salt Creek', about a child.

knows.what: Night one: she had just left Earl's side of the table. She saw it. She knows Cody by more than his name.
knows.tells: Stiles; the deputy, if he has been decent to her in front of the room
knows.takes: Trust first, and then money: she'd take it and it would still be true. Never a threat. Better men have tried.

knows.what: Which of the Baron's riders are new this season, which are paid in gold, and that the hands don't like the new foreman.
knows.tells: the same
knows.takes: The same.

knows.what: The sawn floor: nothing.

saloon_girl.trouble: Nerve 0.6, nosy 0.6, duty 0.4. She gets a table between herself and it and watches the whole of it: she is the best witness in the room. Afterward she goes to the man on the floor; she has torn up a petticoat for a wound before. She would send the boy for the doctor. No gun: a hat pin, and she has used it.

harlan.starts: Wary: a married-looking farmer who doesn't look at her.
harlan.warms: Being spoken to as he would speak to Mrs. Hollis; Cody arrested.
harlan.cools: He sat at that table while Earl was shot, and she saw him sit; being looked through.

greets.warm: Deputy. Sit, I'll not charge you for the tea.
greets.wary: Evening, Deputy. You're not here for the tea.
greets.afraid: I've a child, mister. Whatever it is.

jobs: A section hand owes her four dollars and has told the room she robbed him.
One month's eight dollars never reached Pueblo. She has the stub.
A friend of Cody's comes upstairs and won't leave, and the barkeep says it isn't his business until something is broken.

looks.hair: Dark red-brown, put up with two combs.
looks.clothes: The red dress with the hem mended twice, a shawl for the porch, hair up with two combs.
looks.wear: Powder over a tired face; a burn scar on the left wrist, from the Fire.

casting.voice: Twenties, quick, a little hoarse; Chicago with her mother's Cork in the vowels.
casting.pace: Quick; a little hoarse.

owns.money: A hundred and sixty dollars in a stocking in the mattress, toward four hundred.
owns.home: A trunk, two dresses, a hat she is trimming herself, Nora's tintype in a prayer book.
owns.pockets: A hat pin, a dollar in her shoe, the money order stubs.
owns.owes: The barkeep, a dollar a day for the room, off the top. Mrs. Hollis, nothing.

week.sunday: Sleeps till noon; the creek; the hat. She works that night all the same.
week.payday: The hardest night and the best: forty dollars, if nobody is sick on her.
week.vices: None she can afford. A glass of port on Sunday. Laudanum once, in Denver, and not again.

loyalty.why: She takes the Baron's riders' money and likes none of them. She is afraid of Cody.

townsman.name: Lyman Peck
townsman.who: A town-lot man who bought where the depot was going to be and has stood on the boardwalk ever since, telling the news.
townsman.came: Sold insurance and corner lots through three Kansas boom towns. Came to Salt Creek ahead of the railroad in 'eighty with borrowed money, and bought six lots at the west end. The company put its depot at the other.
townsman.work: None anybody can see: the hotel's walk, the store's bench, the barber's, all day.
townsman.place: A room at the hotel; its porch at dusk.
townsman.wants: One buyer. He would take a note.
townsman.secret: He is three weeks behind with Mrs. Rudd and the note on the lots falls due at the bank this autumn. The clean collar is all the capital he has left.

likes.why: Printed his handbill on credit: 'CHOICE LOTS'.
A man of business; he'd like to be taken for another.

dislikes.why: Says aloud in the street what Mr. Peck says low.
She notices.

townsman.habit: Glances over his shoulder before he tells you anything. Touches his collar.
talks: Low and worried, a Yankee's 'I calculate' and 'I guess'.
Passes on what he was told and who told it; never what he saw.
Never a man's name aloud if the man might be near.
townsman.voice: Forties, low, quick, Connecticut; a salesman's voice with the confidence gone out of it.
townsman.clothes: A town suit worn at the cuffs, a paper collar changed daily, a watch chain with no watch on it.

lines.words: Six lots, west end, fronting where the depot ought to have gone. I calculate the company owes me a depot.
Low, now. That's one of the Baron's riders by the trough, and I'd as soon he didn't know my voice.
A collar, Mrs. Hollis. Only the collar. There's a gentleman coming to look at a lot. He wrote that he might.
The survey stakes run right past my corner. I walked out and looked at them again this morning.
You wouldn't want a lot? Fifty feet on Main. I'd take a note.

fixed.role: the scripts' townsman: 'a storekeeper type; worried, talks low, glances over his shoulder' (No Law, Beat 1)

townsman.notes: He tells the town's news in the scripts (the `townsman` pool is everyone's default too); his own lines here are his.
townsman.in_town: Two years. He came in the spring of 'eighty ahead of the railroad with a carpetbag and borrowed money, bought six lots at the west end, and watched the company put its depot at the east. He's seen the cars come in, the town grow toward the wrong end, and the price of a lot fall by half. Before: insurance at Norwich; corner lots at Abilene, Wichita and Garden City, a boom in each and a bust after.

circle.friends: Mapes, who will talk to him on the store's bench, and he listens. Bérubé, who printed his handbill on credit. The hotel's porch at dusk with whoever is on it. Church on Sundays, because buyers go to church.
circle.family: A wife, Adelia, at Norwich with her father, who wrote last spring that she would join him when he had a house. He hasn't answered.

home.what: A back room at the hotel, three weeks behind; his deeds in a tin trunk under the bed.
home.where: the hotel's lot (not built yet); his six lots at the west end stand empty, with stakes

if_dies.grief: Not much, and he'd have expected more. Mapes misses him most and says so loudest.

lines.words: Mr. Peck bought six lots at the west end ahead of the railroad, and I believe he walked out to look at them every morning, rain or not.
Three weeks, and the room. I'll not ask it of anybody. Saturdays I'd say his name, and he'd touch his collar.
Lyman'd stand there and let me talk, the whole of it. There's nobody else in this town ever— Who am I going to tell it to now? Hollis?
Paper collar, a fresh one. I don't know where he found the dime for it.

if_dies.bearers: Mapes, Yount, Burdett, Colby's hired man, Bérubé; Stroud to the gate. Nobody had to be asked.
if_dies.after: The six lots are sold for the note, to the Baron's agent, for a fifth of what Peck paid. A letter from Norwich comes to the hotel and Mrs. Rudd answers it.

knows.what: Everything he's been told, and who told him. After B3, the town's loose version: 'some stranger on a sorrel'. Before it, 'road agents, or Utes'.
knows.tells: everybody, low, looking over his shoulder
knows.takes: Nothing. It is worth what it cost.

knows.what: That the Baron's agent has been at the county seat's land office asking after lots on the creek side of town. He heard it from a drummer.
knows.tells: the deputy, if he will listen
knows.takes: Listening. It may be true.

knows.what: What he saw himself: almost nothing. He was behind the trough.
The sawn floor: nothing.

townsman.trouble: Nerve 0.2, nosy 0.9, duty 0.1. First behind the trough at the first shot, and first out from behind it when it's over, to tell the street what happened, wrongly. He'll carry if somebody asks him to, because he can't say no to a man's face.

harlan.starts: Warm, too quickly: a deputy might know a buyer.
harlan.warms: Being listened to; being asked; being seen with him on the walk.
harlan.cools: Being told he's wrong in front of the bench; the Baron's riders angry with the town, which is bad for lots.

greets.warm: Deputy! A word. Low, now. I was told something this morning, and I calculate you'll want it.
greets.wary: Morning, Deputy. Nothing I know of. Not a thing.
greets.afraid: Now— now, I only heard it. On the bench. Ask anybody was on the bench.

jobs: Somebody pulled the survey stakes on his corner lots and threw them in the creek. He wants it known it was a crime.
A gentleman has written he may come to look at a lot. Peck wants the deputy there when he does, to show the town is orderly.
Mapes repeated in the saloon something Peck said low on the bench, and now one of the Baron's riders wants a word with him.

looks.hair: Brown, thinning, oiled and combed over.
looks.clothes: A town suit worn at the cuffs, a paper collar changed daily, a watch chain with no watch on it.
looks.wear: Shiny cuffs and elbows; boots polished over cracks.

casting.voice: Forties, low, quick, Connecticut; a salesman's voice with the confidence gone out of it.
casting.pace: Quick and low; louder when he's selling, and then catches himself.

owns.money: Two dollars and some cents, and six lots worth less than the note on them.
owns.home: A tin trunk: deeds, the plat of Salt Creek with his lots inked red, two shirts, a box of collars.
owns.pockets: A handbill, CHOICE LOTS; a pencil; the watch chain; a letter from Norwich unanswered.
owns.owes: Mrs. Rudd, three weeks. The county bank, the note on the lots, due this autumn. Bérubé, for the handbills.

week.sunday: Church, in the second row, where a buyer would see him.
week.payday: On the walk outside the mine office, with handbills. Nobody buys.
week.vices: Talk. A cigar he can't afford, on Saturdays.

loyalty.why: He'd sell to the Baron tomorrow and thank him. The Baron hasn't asked, which is worse than being afraid of him.

loudmouth.name: Rufus Mapes
loudmouth.who: A bullwhacker the railroad put out of work, who carries freight when he's sober and tells the street about it when he isn't.
loudmouth.came: Drove ox teams on the freight roads to the mining camps from fifteen. The cars reached Salt Creek in 'eighty-one and the long hauls stopped; he stopped with them.
loudmouth.work: Freight from the depot to the store's dock, mornings; the store's bench and the saloon's walk after.
loudmouth.place: A shack on the rear lane; the far end of the bar from six.
loudmouth.wants: To be listened to. And twelve yoke of oxen, which nobody will ever hire again.
loudmouth.secret: He owes the barkeep thirty-one dollars and works it off in tales: who bought what, who came in on the noon train, who said what on the bench.

likes.why: Still pours.
Somebody who'll stand and hear it out.

dislikes.why: Pays by the load and counts the sacks twice.
Looked at him once and went on drinking.
A mule man, and says so.

loudmouth.habit: Talks to a man's back as he walks away. Slaps the bench beside him for you to sit.
talks: Loud, and all in one breath: 'I said to him, I said'.
Every story has him in it, in the right.
Never says 'I don't know'.
loudmouth.voice: Thirties, loud, a little thick with drink; Pike County.
loudmouth.clothes: A teamster's check shirt, galluses, a bull whip he still carries coiled on his shoulder, flour on his trousers.

lines.words: Two hundred pound of flour and he wants it up the step gentle. I drove twelve yoke over Mosquito Pass, I reckon I can find a step.
I said to him, I said, you can stop my credit but you can't stop my mouth, and he never had a word to say to that, not a word.
Railroad! Wasn't for the railroad I'd have forty head of oxen and a boy to cuss 'em for me.
Stand me one, Jory, and I'll tell you what the storekeeper's wife said about the widow Rudd.
I ain't drunk. I'm resting, and I been resting since noon, ask anybody.

fixed.role: townsfolk brief §2, roster 15; the scripts' 'bold man in the street': 'a teamster or a hand in town; too loud, a little drunk'

loudmouth.notes: valley_folk.json has his home as the saloon; the roster says a shack on the rear lane. His script lines stand ('Ain't no sheriff tonight, boys!').
loudmouth.in_town: Six years, on and off. Salt Creek was the end of his freight road from 'seventy-six, when it was a store, a smithy and the mine's first adit. He stopped for good when the cars came in 'eighty-one, and sold his last four yoke to a butcher. He has seen all of it change and says he said it would. Before: a bullwhacker from fifteen, Missouri to Santa Fe and then the mountain camps.

circle.friends: Whoever is on the store's bench. Peck, who will stand and listen. The far end of the bar; the Railroad Saloon when the barkeep cuts him off. Fridays he watches the cards and tells the players what they ought to have done.
circle.family: A wife who went back to Pike County in 'seventy-nine and took the boy. A brother who farms there. He sends nothing.

home.what: A one-room shack on the rear lane, behind the saloon.

if_dies.grief: The street is quieter, and people find they don't know the news.

lines.words: Rufus Mapes. He told every man here what was wrong with him, mostly in the street, and he told me twice. He carried my stove up this hill on his back the first winter and wouldn't hear of a dollar.
Thirty-one dollars. Well. That's wrote off.
He would stand and hear a man out. Nobody else in this town... he'd talk after, of course. For an hour. But he heard you first.

if_dies.bearers: Yount, Stroud, Peck, Burdett, the barkeep, and Hollis, who paid him by the load.
if_dies.after: Freight sits two days on the depot's platform, until Hollis hires the drifter. The barkeep has lost his ear on the store's bench.

knows.what: Night one: he was at the far end of the bar, drunk, and saw it through three other men. His telling is wrong in the details and he'll swear to every one.
knows.tells: everybody
knows.takes: Nothing. The work is in the sorting.

knows.what: Whatever comes off the cars: who got down from the noon train with a saddle and no trunk, and whose freight went where.
knows.tells: the barkeep, against his slate; then the street
knows.takes: A drink.

knows.what: The sawn floor: nothing.

loudmouth.trouble: Nerve 0.5, nosy 0.8, duty 0.1. He pushes to the front to see and shouts advice. He is first out of the door when a gun shows, and first back in after. He fetches nobody. He is telling it within the minute, standing nearer than he stood. (Whether he is the loudest man at the rope is not decided.)

harlan.starts: Cold and mocking: a farmer in the sheriff's badge.
harlan.warms: A drink stood him; being let tell it; a fight won where he could watch.
harlan.cools: Being fined, or made small in front of the bench.

greets.warm: Deputy! Here, sit, I was just telling 'em how you done it.
greets.wary: Morning, Deputy! Fine morning for it, ain't it?
greets.cold: You again. Go on by, farmer.
greets.afraid: I never said it! Whoever told you I said it's a liar!

jobs: He swears Hollis shorted him two loads' pay. The book says otherwise.
Somebody sleeps in his shack while he is at the saloon.
The Railroad Saloon holds his bullwhip against six dollars and he wants the law to get it back.

looks.hair: Black, greasy, under a hat with no shape left.
looks.clothes: A teamster's check shirt, galluses, flour on his trousers; the bullwhip coiled on his shoulder when he has it.
looks.wear: Flour and road dust; a drinker's nose.

casting.voice: Thirties, loud, a little thick with drink; Pike County.
casting.pace: Loud and fast, all in one breath.

owns.money: None after Tuesday.
owns.home: A cot, and an ox yoke on the wall that he won't sell.
owns.pockets: Plug tobacco, a cork, a brass check from the freight office.
owns.owes: The barkeep, thirty-one dollars. Hollis, four, advanced. The Railroad Saloon, six.

week.sunday: The saloon's walk and the bench from noon, with a sore head.
week.payday: The Railroad Saloon first, because it is cheaper, then the far end of the bar to tell the miners how they've been cheated.
week.vices: Whiskey: forty-rod at the Railroad Saloon. Talk.

loyalty.side: on the Baron's payroll at one remove, and doesn't know it
loyalty.why: What he tells the barkeep is sold on, and some of it is bought by the foreman.

undertaker.name: Phineas Colby
undertaker.who: The town's undertaker and its carpenter: unhurried, exact, and measuring you while you talk.
undertaker.from: Bath, Maine; a ship joiner's apprentice
undertaker.came: Came out with the rush of 'fifty-nine to build sluices and found men paid better for boxes. Twenty-three years in the Territory and the State, the last five here.
undertaker.work: Planing at his door by day; the dead taken up within the hour; the book. One whiskey at eight.
undertaker.place: His shop at the east end; lives in it.
undertaker.wants: Seasoned black walnut, and a hearse with glass sides.
undertaker.secret: His own is under the bench: walnut, brass handles, made to his measure in 'seventy-nine. He lies down in it of a Sunday to see it still fits.

likes.why: Signs what he saw and no more.
Keeps a burying under the half hour.
Gets a dead man's name right in the paper.

dislikes.why: Six foot one, and will want a wide box.

undertaker.habit: Looks a man over from hat to boots and his lips move: he's taking your length.
talks: Unhurried and precise: feet and inches, dollars and the hour.
Says a dry thing as plain fact and doesn't know it's funny.
Never 'dead' where 'gone' will do, and never guesses a name for the book.
undertaker.voice: Sixties, dry, level; coast of Maine worn down by Colorado.
undertaker.clothes: Black vest, white shirt, sleeves rolled, a folding rule in the vest pocket, shavings on his cuffs.

lines.words: Five foot ten and a half. Near enough. Stand easy, I was only looking.
Pine's four dollars. Walnut I send to Kansas City for. Three weeks, if the cars are running.
One, and the clock says eight. There's a lid to fit by lamplight and I want the hand steady.
Doctor's crossing over. Got his bag. I'd best see what pine I have dry.
Mine's under the bench. Walnut, brass handles. I lie in it Sundays to see it still fits.

fixed.talks: the scripts' cast: 'unhurried, precise, a dry gallows humour he doesn't know he has'; DIALOGUE.md: 'exact'

undertaker.notes: His script lines stand ('Pine box, charged to the county.').
undertaker.in_town: Five years. He came over from Georgetown in 'seventy-seven with a wagon of tools and a coffin he had made to his own measure, when the hotel was going up and there was framing to be had. He framed half the street, the church included, and buried the rest. He's seen the hill fill: forty-one boards and crosses when he came, more now than there are men in the saloon on payday. Before: a ship joiner at Bath; the sluices of 'fifty-nine; boxes ever since.

circle.friends: The doctor, who signs what he saw and no more. Hadley, at every burying. Bérubé, to whom he gives the dead on a Monday, name, age and cause. One whiskey at the bar at eight, alone. A hired man, Swede, who digs.
circle.family: None living. A wife in Maine he left in 'fifty-nine and wrote to for ten years after; the letters stopped coming back. He doesn't know which of them stopped.

home.what: The back of his shop, a bed beside the bench; his own walnut under the bench.

if_dies.grief: There's nobody to take his measure: the doctor does it, and finds it's in the book already. They bury him in his own walnut, which still fits.

lines.words: Mr. Colby brought up this hill every soul I have buried here, and stood at the foot with his watch open.
He'd written his own measure in the book in 'seventy-nine: six foot two. I took it again this morning, for the certificate, and he'd lost half an inch to that bench.
Brass handles, from Kansas City. I'd have made him iron. No charge.
Every Monday: name, age and cause, in his square hand. For his own I have gone to the doctor, and the doctor will not guess the age.

if_dies.bearers: His hired man, the doctor, Yount, Hollis, Bérubé, and Hadley's arm on the box; Stroud to the gate.
if_dies.after: No one makes boxes: the next man goes up the hill in a wagon box, and the county sends to Pueblo for one. The planing at his door stops, and the street is quieter in a way people don't place.

knows.what: The dead, exactly: he lays out everyone. The sheriff, day 2: the ball went in level and close, from a man sitting a horse beside him, the way the doctor said. He gives it to the doctor and the book.
knows.tells: the doctor; the deputy, if asked at the shop
knows.takes: Asking him as a tradesman. He doesn't guess past what he measured.

knows.what: Earl: shot by one Cody, before witnesses (his book's line).
knows.tells: anyone
knows.takes: Nothing.

knows.what: After the floor: shown the girder, he can say at once it was a saw's kerf, a fine-toothed handsaw, new, and not a break: he framed the room's floor. K8 reaches the town at B12 only if someone shows them the cut; he is the one who'd say what it is.
knows.from: after Payday Night, if he is taken to the girder
knows.tells: the deputy, and anyone standing there
knows.takes: Being taken to it. He won't go into the rubble on his own.

knows.what: The strangers' boxes: the boots and pockets of every man nobody claimed, kept a year with the date.
knows.tells: the deputy
knows.takes: Asking for the box by date.

undertaker.trouble: Nerve 0.7, nosy 0.3, duty 0.4. At a shot he steps back inside his door and waits, as he has for twenty years. When it's done he comes out with his rule. At a fire he takes his tools out first, and then helps at the buckets with the carpenter's eye for what will fall. He has never carried a gun.

harlan.starts: Level: he takes the deputy's length, as anyone's.
harlan.warms: Bringing the dead in decently; a name found for a stranger; the county billed and not a widow.
harlan.cools: Bodies left in the street; strangers shot with nobody to say who they were.

greets.warm: Morning, Deputy. Five foot eleven, near enough. You're keeping well.
greets.wary: Deputy. Is it business?
greets.cold: Deputy. I'll be at the bench, if it's the county's business.
greets.afraid: I only bury them. I don't— You'd want the doctor.

jobs: A year's up on a stranger's boots. There was a letter in the pocket from a woman in Trinidad: he'd like the deputy to write to her before he burns it.
Walnut planks gone from his yard, eight feet each. He knows the measure exactly, and would know them anywhere.
A body up a draw on the East Road, two weeks dead, the county wants fetched, and he won't go alone.

looks.hair: White, cut short, a cowlick he wets.
looks.clothes: Black vest, white shirt, sleeves rolled, a folding rule in the vest pocket, shavings on his cuffs.
looks.wear: Shavings on his cuffs; a carpenter's flat thumb; a pencil behind each ear.

casting.voice: Sixties, dry, level; coast of Maine worn down by Colorado.
casting.pace: Unhurried; precise with numbers.

owns.money: The county's warrants, unpaid, three hundred dollars of them; forty in coin.
owns.home: His shop and its tools, seasoned pine, a little walnut, his own box, the book of the dead since 'seventy-seven.
owns.pockets: A folding rule, a pencil, a watch he winds at eight.
owns.owes: Nothing. The county owes him.

week.sunday: Church at ten; in the afternoon he lies down in his own box to see it still fits.
week.payday: Payday nights are business. One whiskey at eight, as always.
week.vices: One whiskey at eight, by the clock.

loyalty.why: He bills the county for everybody, the Baron's men too. He has buried two of the ranch's riders this year and noted where they were shot from.

runner.role: The young man the doctor sends
runner.name: Caleb Rudd
runner.who: The landlady's boy, sixteen, who runs the doctor's errands and hangs about the depot to watch the telegraph key.
runner.from: Lockport, New York; in Salt Creek since he was eleven
runner.came: With his mother and father when the hotel was built.
runner.work: Errands, wood and water for the doctor at fifty cents a week; the hotel's slops.
runner.place: The hotel; the doctor's back door; the depot when he can get away.
runner.wants: To be a telegraph operator. The depot agent lets him hold the key.
runner.secret: He saw a man's leg taken off in the doctor's front room, held the lamp for it, and hasn't told his mother.

likes.why: Talks to him as if he were a man.
Lets him work the bellows.

dislikes.why: Calls him 'sonny' and sends him for tobacco.

runner.habit: Runs everywhere, and stops dead to listen when the wire clicks or the whistle goes.
talks: Quick, half sentences, 'sir' and 'ma'am'.
Railroad time and the doctor's words, both got slightly wrong.
Never swears where his mother might hear of it, which is everywhere.
runner.voice: Sixteen, a voice not long broken, quick.
runner.clothes: His father's vest taken in, trousers too short, a cap, a doctor's apron when he's been called in a hurry.

seen.when: day 2: the doctor sends him to find you

lines.words: Harlan! Doc's asking for you.
Doc has me wash in the carbolic. Hands, to the elbow. Then he looks, and I do it over.
Ma, the noon train's nine minutes down. The agent let me hold the key.
Can't stop, mister. Doc's got me after ice, and there ain't any nearer than the butcher's.
Fifty cents a week and I seen a man's leg come off. Ma don't know about the leg.

fixed.role: valley_folk.json: the young man the doctor sends on day 2 (SheriffDies)

runner.notes: He has no day in valley_folk.json (an act man); the brief's runner (whoever fetches the doctor) is any townsman with duty.
runner.in_town: Five years: he came at eleven with his mother and father in 'seventy-seven, and helped carry his father up the hill at twelve. He's seen everything the town has, at a run: the cars come in, the depot and its key, the doctor's front room. Before: Lockport, where he remembers the canal and nothing else.

circle.friends: The doctor. Stroud, on the bellows. The depot agent, who lets him hold the key. The section gang's boys, at the water tower. Mapes calls him sonny and he'd like to fight him.
circle.family: His mother. His father on the hill. An aunt in Rochester he's to be sent to if he doesn't find a trade.

home.what: A cot in the room off the hotel's kitchen, next to his mother's.

if_dies.grief: Mrs. Rudd closes the hotel for the first time. The doctor does his own errands and is late for them. The depot agent sends a message down the line that nobody asked him to send.

lines.words: Caleb Rudd, sixteen. He went past my gate a dozen times a day, running, with something for the doctor in his hand.
He held the lamp for me through an amputation in March and it didn't shake. His mother didn't know.
That's his father's vest. I took it in for him in March.
Talked the whole time on them bellows. I'd tell him quit and he'd quit for about a minute.

if_dies.bearers: Stroud, who comes through the gate for him, the doctor, Trembath, Yount, Colby, and the depot agent.
if_dies.after: The doctor has nobody to send. Mrs. Rudd sells the hotel by spring. Cornelius's boots go up the hill with her, or stay by the kitchen door for the next owner to find.

knows.what: The doctor's front room on day 2: Earl's body on the table under a sheet, and the doctor's word that the sheriff isn't to know (S50). He held the lamp.
knows.tells: nobody: the doctor told him not to
knows.takes: The doctor's leave.

knows.what: The wires: he hears the agent read them off. PROPOSED, for Sean: the captain's wire, the morning it comes (I Am the Law), before the street has it, got slightly wrong.
knows.tells: everybody, at a run
knows.takes: Nothing; he can't keep it.

knows.what: Every horse that came through on the East Road while he was at the depot. He doesn't know whose.
knows.tells: the deputy
knows.takes: Being asked like a man.

knows.what: The sawn floor: nothing.

runner.trouble: Nerve 0.5, nosy 0.9, duty 0.7. He runs for the doctor before anyone says so, and then runs back to see, and gets too close. At a fire he's on the bucket line, then up a ladder he shouldn't be on. He's never held a gun and would like to.

harlan.starts: Warm: he ran to fetch him on day 2, and the deputy came.
harlan.warms: Being sent on an errand; being told something first; being called by his name.
harlan.cools: Being sent home to his mother; seeing a man shot who had his hands up.

greets.warm: Deputy! Doc's in. You want something run? I'm quick.
greets.wary: Morning, sir. Can't stop.
greets.cold: Ma says I'm not to talk to you.
greets.afraid: I wasn't— I was only at the depot, sir. You ask the agent.

jobs: The agent says a telegram went missing between the key and the hotel, and Caleb carried it.
Mapes called him sonny in front of the section boys. His mother asks the deputy to stop the fight before it happens.
He found a saddled horse loose on the East Road and has hidden it in the doctor's shed, hoping to be paid for it.

looks.hair: Tow-coloured, cut by his mother with a bowl.
looks.clothes: His father's vest taken in, trousers too short, a cap, a doctor's apron when he's been called in a hurry.
looks.wear: Scrubbed red hands to the elbow; carbolic smell; scabbed knees through the trousers.

casting.voice: Sixteen, a voice not long broken, quick.
casting.accent: Upstate New York gone Colorado: his mother's vowels, the section boys' grammar.
casting.pace: Quick, half sentences, out of breath.

owns.money: Two dollars and a quarter in a sock, toward a telegraph key of his own.
owns.home: A cot, a box with his father's pocket knife, a Morse table copied out in pencil.
owns.pockets: A dime for holding a horse, a piece of telegraph wire, the doctor's list.
owns.owes: Nothing. The doctor owes him a week.

week.sunday: Church with his mother, fidgeting. The depot in the afternoon, to see the train.
week.payday: Holding horses outside the saloon for dimes until his mother finds him.
week.vices: A chaw behind the livery, once, which made him sick.

loyalty.why: The Baron's riders give him a dime to hold a horse and he thinks their horses are the finest in the valley. He'd go over to anyone who gave him a gun.

cody.name: Cody
cody.who: The man who kills Earl in front of the saloon on night one, and later the one witness who can tie the Baron to it.
cody.from: Texas (the script's brief: 'a Texas cowhand gone bad')
cody.place: The saloon when he's in town; then Harlan's cell, and the depot's freight room.
cody.secret: He knows who shot the sheriff, who raided the camp, and who pays.
talks: Loud and short; brave with drink in him and a crew behind him.
In the cell: sullen, then frightened, then bargaining.
One of the few men allowed a slur (C13 b), only where it matters.
cody.voice: Late twenties, a hard flat voice, a sneer in it.

seen.when: night 1 (No Law); again after the funeral, when Harlan arrests him

lines.words: Earl, you cheating son of a bitch!
Ain't no law left in this valley to save you now, Earl.
You're the law, ain't you? Then it's on you to keep me breathing.

stranger.role: The stranger at the table, who is the Baron's foreman
stranger.who: The Baron's new foreman: he shot the sheriff from the saddle, and on night one he sits down at Harlan's table to learn what the sheriff said.
stranger.came: New to the valley this season (proposed in the bible), which is why the sheriff didn't know him.
stranger.work: The Baron's foreman: he pays the men and runs the errands.
stranger.place: The Baron's ranch; a bald-faced sorrel at the saloon's rail.
stranger.wants: To know whether the sheriff could talk.
stranger.secret: He shot the sheriff. And he is a coward: he fired once and rode, which is why the man lived a day. Held back for a mid-game reveal; nobody says the word.
stranger.habit: Asks leave for what he means to do anyway.
talks: Soft-spoken and mannerly; 'friend', then 'Deputy' with a smile.
The tenser it gets, the more courteous.
'Ain't' when it suits him.
stranger.voice: About fifty, Western, low; never hurried, never raised.

seen.when: the funeral, a step behind the Baron, saying nothing
the widow's lane, with the deed

lines.words: Evening. Mind if I sit in a while?
Don't move, friend. Whatever happens next, you sit still.
I'll say good night, friend. Anybody asks, I'd take it kindly if you'd been looking into your glass.

stranger.notes: Two roster ids, one man: `stranger` (No Law) and `foreman` (the funeral).

dying_sheriff.who: The county sheriff, fourteen years on his claim east of town; shot over his water before dawn on day one, dead on day two whatever Harlan does.
dying_sheriff.from: A plains man, Missouri or Kansas (the script's brief)
dying_sheriff.came: Took up his claim in 1868 and cut its ditch with a spade and a borrowed mule.
dying_sheriff.place: His claim east of town; then the doctor's cot; then his grave.
dying_sheriff.wants: His wife and boys looked to.
dying_sheriff.habit: Gives orders, even on his back.
talks: Orders; plain, dry, no wasted word.
Calls a man of forty 'son'.
As he loses blood the sentences shorten; short of breath, not quiet.
dying_sheriff.voice: Early fifties, low and dry, gravel from pain; never a whisper until the very end.

lines.words: Well? Nod or don't, but don't just stand there.
That ain't how it's done, son.
The Baron's wanted that ditch since the day I cut it. He'll go at my wife for it now. Look to her and the boys.

wife.role: The sheriff's wife, then his widow
wife.who: The sheriff's wife: the claim and its creek right are hers now, with two young sons and a dog, Blue. She won't sell.
wife.from: A Midwestern farm wife with good schooling (the script's brief)
wife.work: The claim: the stock, the ditch, the gate.
wife.place: The homestead east of town; in town on day two and at the funeral.

dislikes.why: He made his offer at the grave.

talks: Straight and short; hard questions, not softened.
Dry when she's easy, cold when she isn't.
'Mr. Harlan', always.
wife.voice: About forty, level and low, short; grief held under work.

lines.words: Were you with him?
He's not covered over yet.
My husband cut that ditch with a spade and a borrowed mule. That man can offer till he's hoarse.

fixed.name: roles only (C14 c)
fixed.who: VOICES.md (D); no romance with Harlan, ever

baron.who: The valley's cattle Baron: he wants every drop of water in it, and he is patient.
baron.from: Eastern or British money; his accent is Sean's call
baron.place: A masonry town house on the rise west of town; a ranch to the south-east.
baron.wants: Every drop of water in the valley.
baron.secret: The plan: make the town look in revolt, so the Army comes.

dislikes.why: For the botched job on the road (proposed in the bible).

baron.habit: Remembers names. Offers to buy before he takes.
talks: Educated, courteous, unhurried; long sentences where everyone else is short.
Never a threat in words: prices, and regrets.

town_drunk.role: The town drunk, an old soldier

town_drunk.called: Sarge, by the whole town, and none of them mean it kindly but the preacher
town_drunk.who: A broken first sergeant of the Union army, drunk by noon, who mocks the deputy every time he lays eyes on him and is right about him more often than he's funny.
town_drunk.from: Sangamon County, Illinois; a wheelwright's son
town_drunk.came: Mustered out a private in 'sixty-five with a pension he drank and a trade his hands had forgotten. Drove a team for the Army's posts in Kansas, then for the mine's first freight in 'seventy-six, and was let go the same winter for being found asleep under the wagon.

First shot you hear in earnest, Brevet, you'll shit yer britches. Every man does. I done it at Shiloh, and I was a sergeant.
You walk like a man with the quickstep and no sink dug. Ease off, Brevet, nobody's shooting yet.
That your pistol, or you minding it for the sheriff? T'other end, farmer. The hole goes forward.
I seen better law on a privy door. That had a latch on it, anyhow.
Brevet! Your drawers is showing. No, t'other pair. The pair you'll want changing by sundown.
Took a ball in the seat at Shiloh. Going forward! I'd bent for my cap. Surgeon said it was the one part of me he could find to hit.
Stand a veteran a drink. I bled for this country. Out the hind end, mind, but it come out red.
Give us 'Dixie', Johnny! Go on. I never could hear it but from the far side of a fence.

He has seen the town from the ground up, mostly from the ground: the store when it was the only front, the sheriff ride in from his claim on court days, the hotel, the graders' camp, the cars, and the Baron's riders begin to come in armed. Before: a wheelwright's shop in Sangamon County; four years in an Illinois infantry regiment, first sergeant of his company by Shiloh and a private by Chattanooga; ten years driving for Army posts in Kansas.

circle.family: A wife, Hannah, in Illinois, who had him declared dead in 'seventy-one and married a harness-maker, and was right to. A daughter he has not seen since she was four. Nobody in town knows of either.

lines.words: Ephraim Tolliver, First Sergeant, of an Illinois regiment. I have that from the Pension Office; I wrote to them this week, for it seemed somebody should. He was drunk every day I knew him, and the only thing he ever asked me for was the time of day.
He swept that floor for what was left in the glasses. I'd leave a finger in a few. Don't nobody tell that round.
Same field, him and me, from the two ends of it. I'll play him that Yankee tune of his. In time, too, which he'd say I couldn't.
Plate came back washed. Every night. It's on the step tonight; I put it out before I remembered.

A man of about thirty. Five foot nine. A scar across the left hand. He goes in the book as a stranger.
I keep the boots and what was in the pockets a year, in a box with the date on it. In 'seventy-nine a woman wrote from Ohio, and I sent her a knife and a tintype.
Drank in my place twice. Rye, paid in silver. Sat by the stove.

rider.words: They tell me he rode for wages with the men who did the shooting. What he did with his own hand I don't know. Nobody has come up this hill for him but Mr. Colby and me.
Nobody claimed the horse either. The county has it, against the box.
His friends rode right by my door going out. Ary one of 'em could've stopped.

outlaw.words: {name}. This town knows what he did, and I'll not stand here and say otherwise over him. He is in other hands than ours now, and I am content to leave him there.
I am told to say some good of the dead. He was somebody's boy once, I suppose. We'll go on to the prayer.
{name}. Shot, before witnesses. I have buried two that he sent me, and he goes in beside them, as there's no other row dug.
Hand me the shovel. Somebody else can say the words over him; I'll be at the wagon.
I came up to see him put under, and so I have. Amos will want his supper.
